# **Final Report**

Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor

Sponsor: Peter Chen

![][image1]

Dylan Bailes, Kaitlyn Lavarias, Dylan Lee, Samantha Olivar  
MAE 156B \- Fundamental Principles of Mechanical Design II  
University of California San Diego  
Professor David Gillett  
RELEASE \- 6/7/2026

# **Abstract** {#abstract}

	This project, sponsored by researcher Dr. Peter Chen, provided a research platform for analyzing stem cell differentiation behavior in the presence of external stimuli. Upon the application of various stimuli, stem cells can be encouraged to switch to different development modes in a process called differentiation, allowing them to be used for applications like limb regrowth or other regenerative medical procedures. Exposure to electric and magnetic fields is a stimulus that has proven effects; however the data on what exactly those effects are is ambiguous. To investigate this, the engineered Multi-Chamber-Camera Bioreactor (MCCB) housed multiple stem cell cultures inside wells filled with saline fluid and subjected them to controlled electric fields via titanium electrodes and magnetic fields through Helmholtz electromagnet coils. The wells were designed to be manufactured using the Stratasys polyjet 3D printer. This allowed for custom features like slots for the electrodes, a threaded and sealable lid, as well as mating features for luer locks that allow the user to manually add additional saline fluid during the experiment. Individual camera-microscope modules on fine-control 3-axis gantry systems were positioned below each well, allowing clear vision at specific points of interest inside each cell culture. Finally, a touchscreen interface controlled and monitored the stimuli to each of the different wells. The team confirmed through voltage mapping and magnetometer measurements that the MCCB produced electric fields between 0-1.5 V/cm and magnetic fields between 0-5 mT. Ultimately, the project successfully delivered a fully validated, functional platform for stem cell research.

#  **Chapter 1: Project Description** {#chapter-1:-project-description}

## ***Project Background*** {#project-background}

Bioreactors are tools used by bioengineers to maintain a controlled environment for living matter to invoke a biological reaction. For this project, the goal is to create a small-scale, affordable bioreactor. Two specific stimuli, electric field and magnetic field, will be applied to the cells through the bioreactor. This project’s sponsor, Dr. Peter Chen, has a background in bioengineering and an interest in exploring the effects of these two stimuli on stem cells. He is pursuing research for the use of stem cells in regenerative medical procedures, and is following up on the research of a previous team that had utilized a simplified bioreactor to verify the influence of electric fields on stem cell development.  
Stem cells are cells in the body that do not have a designated function, so they are capable of self-duplicating or differentiating into specialized cells such as heart or blood cells. By stimulating stem cells with electric and magnetic fields, Dr. Chen will be able to conduct different experiments that observe the effects on the differentiation of these cells and, in the future, use this data to achieve fine and intentional control over the differentiation process.  
A previous team attempted to meet Dr. Chen’s requests but was unsuccessful in providing a usable tool to allow for the proper imaging of cells under the influence of the target stimuli. The previous team’s project did not allow for accessible viewing of the cells considering Dr. Chen’s equipment. The system was also difficult to interact with and sterilize, and presented many obstacles with acute stimuli control. With this project, the final deliverable is a tool that allows Dr. Chen to both control the magnitude of input stimuli and microscopically image the effects on stem cells.

## ***Review of Existing Design Solutions***

### **Existing Bioreactors** {#existing-bioreactors}

#### **Bioreactors as Tools for Controlling Stem Cells**

#### Bioreactors are designed to support and control biological processes. Various existing designs focus on maintaining conditions for cell growth by controlling temperature, pH, or nutrient supply. However, in the context of stem cell engineering, modern bioreactors attempt to play a role in controlling the differentiation of stem cells through precise control of biochemical and biophysical stimuli.

![][image2]

##### **Figure 1.1 Different types of traditional bioreactors categorized by component input.** {#figure-1.1-different-types-of-traditional-bioreactors-categorized-by-component-input.}

#### To understand the existing solutions relating to current bioreactors, it is essential to look at how different systems manage fluids as this dictates both the complexity of the hardware, but also the degree of control that researchers have over the cell culture. There are three types of traditional bioreactors: batch, fed-batch, or continuous systems as seen in Figure 1.1. \[1\] Batch systems involve all components being input at the beginning with no additional inputs added during the process, effectively making the system closed. This design is one of the simplest in terms of being inexpensive and easy to set up, while also being low maintenance and having little risk for contamination. However, batch bioreactors limit the dynamic control over the cells because researchers cannot actively adjust the environment.

#### Fed-batch systems improve on this design by allowing for the addition of nutrients during the cultivation process. The addition of nutrients throughout observation replenishes the food for the cells to grow and extends the lifespan of the target cells. Comparatively it has increased complexity with the required hardware and volume management.

#### Continuous systems provide steady-state operation and consistent environmental conditions. In regard to being able to reproduce results and having the most control over the environment, a continuous system is the ideal bioreactor design. However, the system would be more complex and sensitive to contamination, considering the need to incorporate feedback to ensure accurate control of the different stimuli.

Stem cells are useful in bioengineering research because of their ability to self-renew and differentiate, making them sensitive to their surrounding environment. Therefore, in order to stimulate stem cells successfully, bioreactors must both expand stem cell populations and also guide their differentiation into specific cells with consistency \[2\].

### **Manufacturing methods and sterilization of cell wells** {#manufacturing-methods-and-sterilization-of-cell-wells}

Cell culture wells are typically manufactured from biocompatible materials such as glass, stainless steel, or polymer based plastics, depending on whether the well is intended to be reusable or single-use. Reusable systems are designed to withstand repeated sterilization cycles and are commonly sterilized using steam autoclaving. The process of steam autoclaving applies a high temperature, high pressure steam to eliminate contaminants \[3\]. Single use wells are pre-sterilized and can be disposed of in plastic culture bags. Single use options are easily replaceable and eliminate the need for autoclaving.  
In the case that resin is the desired material for a cell culture well, while there are biocompatible resins, most resin is not. Therefore, before being used as cell culture wells, post-processing using a solution of concentrations of 10–30% NaOH, 1–3% Na2SiO3, 60–80% Na2CO3 proves effective in removing the toxicity of the resin \[4\].

### **Electric Field Generators** {#electric-field-generators}

Electric field generation typically consists of a system containing electrodes, a power supply, and a control system that is designed to deliver electrical cues to the cell. Electric fields can interact with cells by altering membrane potentials, ion transport, and intracellular signalling pathways.   
A sample design of an electric field generator for a bioreactor includes parallel electrodes, creating a controlled electric field across the desired region of observation. Key design characteristics include electrode placement, applied voltage, and electrode conductivity \[5\].  
![][image3]

##### **Figure 1.2 Electric fields between two electrodes submerged in the cell culture \[5\]** {#figure-1.2-electric-fields-between-two-electrodes-submerged-in-the-cell-culture-[5]}

As seen in Figure 1, electrodes are often directly immersed in a culture medium, therefore, to avoid erosion, researchers will use metals such as platinum, gold, titanium, or silver. In Altamirano et al.’s electrode system, using platinum wires and a current around 11.5 nA/mm^2, they were able to stimulate nerve cells at frequencies around 2-3 Hz \[6\]. Additionally, Meng’s research emphasizes that the interactions between the electrode and the medium must be carefully considered, as undesired reactions at the electrode surface can alter local pH or generate unwanted byproducts. As a result, material selection and current regulation are critical design considerations.  
Electrodes made of platinum or silver wires are a modified geometry application of typical capacitor designs that use two oppositely charged plates to generate a uniformly distributed electric field between the plates. While the electric fields are not exactly uniform between two wires used as electrodes, in most biological cell applications, the shape of the field is sufficiently uniform within the tolerances set by the researcher. More advanced systems combine electrical simulation with controlled flow. For example, designs using carbon or metal electrodes embedded in the chamber allow for the simultaneous delivery of nutrients and electrical stimulation. These systems have demonstrated improved cellular organization.

### **Magnetic Field Generators** {#magnetic-field-generators}

There are several existing technologies used in various lab conditions that are relevant to our task of providing uniform magnetic fields. Some common solution methods include using Helmholtz coils and Maxwell coils in research and precision engineering contexts.  
	Helmholtz coils consist of two identical circular coils placed coaxially and separated by a distance equal to their radius. When equal current flows through the coils in the same direction the superposition of their fields produces a region of nearly uniform magnetic field at the midpoint between them. This is often used due to the simple design and effectiveness at creating predictable well characterized fields in a small central volume. However, the region of uniformity is still limited in size and the fields they create are rather weak, requiring significant current for strong field strength which can result in significant heat generation \[8\]. As well as their open geometry of 3D coils can present a challenge to integrate into bioreactor systems.  
	Maxwell coils serve as an extension of Helmholtz coils by introducing a third coil which is positioned between the two outer coils on the same axis. In addition, it also changes the geometry relations between the coils needing the outer coils to be of radius 47R and distance 37R. The outer coils must have exactly 49/64 turns of the larger. This results in a larger geometry over which the field is uniform, but at the cost of a more complex integration and calibration.  
	Both of these represent viable methods of generating controlled uniform magnetic fields for bioreactor like designs, but also present limitations of bulkiness, power consumption and thermal effects.  
![][image4]

##### **Figure 1.3: Helmholtz Coil Geometry and Field Superposition** {#figure-1.3:-helmholtz-coil-geometry-and-field-superposition}

![][image5]

##### **Figure 1.4: Maxwell Coil Geometry** {#figure-1.4:-maxwell-coil-geometry}

### **2021 UCSD MAE 156B Cell Growth Bioreactor** {#2021-ucsd-mae-156b-cell-growth-bioreactor}

	In 2021, Dr. Peter Chen sponsored a senior capstone project with requirements similar to those of this project, including the application of electric and magnetic fields, fluid input and output systems, and a method for controlling these inputs. The primary failures identified in the previous design were as follows: An oversized chamber that prevented effective imaging of the cells with a microscope, a bulky design that was difficult to clean, and an unnecessarily difficult cell loading process.  
![][image6]

##### **Figure 1.5: 2021 UCSD Senior Capstone Design for the Cell Growth Bioreactor for tissue regeneration** {#figure-1.5:-2021-ucsd-senior-capstone-design-for-the-cell-growth-bioreactor-for-tissue-regeneration}

	For the generation of electric fields, they utilized two platinum wires placed in parallel which generated a relatively uniform field directly between the wires, but ultimately had higher field magnitudes closer to the wires. To generate the magnetic field, a singular coil around 13 cm in diameter was used above the chamber, cooled by a large fan. Additional features that will not be considered for the scope of this project are the pressure and flow rate into the chambers controlled by fluid pumps. The user interface for this bioreactor featured adjustability for each of the inputs and plots that graphed the monitored variable over time.

## ***Statement of Requirements and Deliverables***

### **Functional Requirements:** {#functional-requirements:}

1. Have a minimum of 4 chambers/wells to hold the cell cultures  
   1. Chambers must have an optically clear bottom that allows observation by a microscope  
      1. The well bottom shall be constructed of a material that has \>95% light transmission and \< 2% haze.  
      2. The well bottom must have a thickness of less than the focal length of the microscope (\< 5 mm)  
   2. Chambers must be sealable with no visible bubbles forming underwater at 10 psi air input  
   3. Each chamber must be minimum 1 cm in height and 1.5 cm in diameter  
   4. All materials in the well design must be compatible with other components of the MCCB  
      1. Anything in contact with the cell culture shall be certified non-toxic to cells, meeting ISO 10993-5 standards.  
      2. Components of the design must have minimal interference (𝜇r \< 1.05) with the magnetic field applied to the cells  
2. Optics  
   1. Microscope and camera assembly must provide resolution to view zebrafish embryos which are approximately 25 micrometers in diameter  
   2. For proper illumination to view the cell samples, either white light or green light in the 550 nm wavelength must be integrated in the well  
      1. A light diffuser must be placed in front of the light for even illumination across the cell culture sample  
3. Magnetic Field applied on cells  
   1. At minimum the magnetic field should be 1.5 mT  
      1. The magnetic field must be relatively uniform across the cell culture sample  
      2. Individual magnetic fields applied to each well must be contained to not interfere significantly with the conditions for neighboring wells  
4. Electric Field applied to applied on cells  
   1. 1.5 V/cm \+/- 10 mV/cm  
      1. Must remain below 1.5 V/cm to avoid risk of unintended electrolysis from occurring  
5. Add+remove fluid from well during experiment  
   1. Manual control by fluid syringes  
   2. Wells must have a fluid exit route (pressure relief). Finalized details TBD by sponsor  
6. Gantry system to move 4 microscopes  
   1. Must allow for 3 DOF (xyz) translation of 4 individual camera and microscope assemblies   
      1. Maximum travel per step: 0.1mm  
   2. Microscope-camera module selection TBD by sponsor

### **Statement of Deliverables:** {#statement-of-deliverables:}

1. Physical Prototype Reactor Hardware  
   1. Four chamber bioreactor structural frame (T-slot extrusion)  
   2. VeroClear resin printed wells  
   3. Titanium plate electrodes for capacitive electric field stimulation  
   4. Helmholtz coil pair electromagnet and Horseshoe core prototype  
   5. Custom PCB with Integrated feedback control using Hall-effect sensors  
   6. Self contained touchscreen for experiment control and visualization  
   7. Fluid inlet and outlet ports for feeding of cells  
2. Simulations  
   1. Electric field Ansys simulation for saline mixture  
   2. Magnetic field Ansys and Python field simulations comparing horseshoe and Helmholtz geometries  
3. Characterization Experiments and Validation Data  
   1. Magnetic Field Uniformity  
      1. Iron filling field visualization  
      2. Hall sensor verification vs predicted magnetic field  
      3. Thermal generation over runtime  
      4. Cross well isolation evaluations  
   2. Electric Field Uniformity  
      1. Multimeter probe mapping for inter electrode distances  
   3. Image Resolution and Clarity  
      1. USAF 1951 resolution test  
      2. Sample images of zebrafish embryo  
   4. Chamber Seal  
      1. Liquid and leak testing  
      2. Pressure Drop validation under operational conditions  
4. Documentation and Reproducibility  
   1. Comprehensive Bill of Materials (BOM) with cost, vendor and part number for all components used  
   2. CAD files, technical drawings, assembly methods, PCB schematics, and firmware repository  
   3. Instructional manual, calibration procedures, and maintenance needs  
   4. Final technical report with design path, test data, and conclusions

# **Chapter 2: Description of Final Design Solution** {#chapter-2:-description-of-final-design-solution}

## ***Design Solution![][image7]*** {#design-solution}

##### **Figure 2.1 Functional Block Diagram of the Multi-Chamber-Camera Bioreactor System** {#figure-2.1-functional-block-diagram-of-the-multi-chamber-camera-bioreactor-system}

##### 

Figure 2.1 outlines the interaction between all the system components included in the Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor design (referred to as the MCCB from here on). The physical system of the MCCB holds the cell cultures in a configuration that allows them to be subjected to electric and magnetic fields. Inlets and outlets in the wells allow for fluidic cell cultures to be manually inserted into the chambers using a syringe. The user interface (referred to the UI from here on) on a touch screen allows the user to dictate the magnitude of electric and magnetic fields applied to the cell cultures, also allowing for the individual control of each of the four wells within the MCCB. In order to monitor the electric field and magnetic field current sensors and hall-effect sensors provide feedback to the UI to inform and calibrate the user input settings. Microscopes with camera attachments are placed under each of the four wells of cell cultures to image the effects on the target cells over time, allowing for automated imaging via the user interface touchscreen.

![][image8]

##### **Figure 2.2 Full CAD Assembly of the MCCB** {#figure-2.2-full-cad-assembly-of-the-mccb}

	Figure 2.2 shows the full assembly for the CAD Design of the MCCB. The primary frame consists of T-Slot rods connected by corner gussets on which a plate of acrylic is used to mount the wells and Helmholtz coils. Directly below each well configuration is a microscope lens attached to an xyz linear stage with a fabricated microscope mount that allows the cable for the attached camera to trail out from underneath the microscope. 

![][image9]![][image10]

##### **Figure 2.3 CAD Assembly of the Cell Culture well Inside the Helmholz coils.** {#figure-2.3-cad-assembly-of-the-cell-culture-well-inside-the-helmholz-coils.}

	Figure 2.3 provides a more detailed view of one of the cell culture assemblies housed within the Helmholtz coil. The 3D resin printed well sits on a lip that aligns the bottom edge of the lid with the bottom edge of the top coil. Copper is wound around each of the coils to generate current, and a PCB board consisting of a hall sensor is mounted to the coils to monitor the magnetic field within the coils. Figure 2.4 shows a labeled assembly of the well components, highlighting the titanium plate electrodes slotted into the wall of the chamber and the o-ring in the dovetail groove on the top face. The square impression on the bottom of the well leaves room for a cover glass slide that will provide optical clarity to allow for clear microscope imaging.

![][image11]

##### **Figure 2.4 Full exploded view of the cell culture well and the lid** {#figure-2.4-full-exploded-view-of-the-cell-culture-well-and-the-lid}

	Figure 2.4 also shows a CAD model of the well lid. The threads interface with the well body to provide a waterproof seal. The luer lock threads provide inlets and outlets for fluid, while the center impression holds the light source to illuminate the cell culture as it is imaged from the bottom.

![][image12]

##### **Figure 2.5 Full physical assembly** {#figure-2.5-full-physical-assembly}

	Figure 2.5 is the assembly completed minus the 3 additional camera-microscope systems which the sponsor will add himself. Everything is held together in a chassis made from 30mm x 30mm x 18in t-slot aluminum extrusion. Extra stock is left on the vertical beams to allow for height adjustability in the event that the microscope stackup changes. The frame is held together using 90 degree aluminum corner gussets and t-gussets made for 3030 t-slot extrusion, with M6 bolts and sliding nuts t-slot nuts fastening the assembly together. The four manually adjustable 3-axis tables are secured using M4 bolts and sliding T-nuts to extrusions that span the base of the assembly. Currently, each table is equidistant from the center and 10 in apart from each other. Since the fastening hardware is sliding, this distancing can be adjusted to be closer together if desired.  
	The remaining bio-related hardware is located on the top of the chassis, where an acrylic plate was laser cut with holes and mounting features. The plate is fastened to the chassis using M6 bolts and sliding T-nuts. Longer M6 Nylon bolts and nuts fasten each printed ASA electrode to the acrylic sheet, and are plastic to avoid eddy currents in steel bolts. The cell culture well and lid screw into each other and are inserted into the electromagnet, where a small outcrop in the print allows the flange to rest on it and be fixed in place. Holes cut in the top of the acrylic serve as mounting points for the custom PCBs that control the electrode and electromagnet.  
![][image13]  
\=

##### **Figure 2.6 High Level Control System Layout** {#figure-2.6-high-level-control-system-layout}

	Figure 2.6 presents a high level layout of the control system that allows users to dictate the exact magnitudes of stimuli and manage viewing and recording of the cells through the camera. The entire system is controlled by a Master Raspberry Pi Controller that connects all the different components that are wired to their respective control boards. The UI uses the React library and various websockets to run on a localhost port on the Pi display and provides graphs of the magnetic and electric fields and feedback from key sensors. The user is easily able to set precise stimuli values across different wells, as well as stop well stimuli when needed and calibrate the control system beforehand.

## ***Cell Culture Well, Lid, and Electrodes*** {#cell-culture-well,-lid,-and-electrodes}

	The cell culture well plays a crucial role in the full MCCB assembly as it holds the cell culture that is the target of observation. As pictured in figure 2.4, the bottom impression in the resin well holds a cover glass slide that allows for optical clarity. Pockets within the well hold electrodes that are powered by a wire fed through the side of the well. To generate a waterproof seal, an O-ring is placed in a groove on the top face of the well. The lid twists onto the well to seal the chamber and houses fluid ports and a light source that illuminate the sample for bottom-viewing by a microscope. The electrodes within the well generate an electric field ranging from 2-5 V/m.

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements}

1. Chambers must have an optically clear bottom that allows observation by  microscope  
   1. The well bottom shall be constructed of a material that has \>95% light transmission and \< 2% haze.  
   2. The well bottom must have a thickness of less than the focal length of the microscope (\< 5 mm)  
2. Chambers must be sealable with no visible bubbles forming underwater at 10 psi air input  
3. Each chamber must be a minimum of 1 cm in height and 1.5 cm in diameter  
4. Anything in contact with the cell culture shall be certified non-toxic to cells, meeting ISO 10993-5 standards.  
5. All materials in the well design must be compatible with other components of the MCCB  
   1. Components of the design must have minimal interference (𝜇r \< 1.05) with the magnetic field applied to the cells  
6. Electrodes must generate an electric field   
   1. Generated electric field must target 2-5 V/cm \+/- 10 mV/cm  
   2. Electric field must remain below 5 V/cm to avoid risk of unintended electrolysis occurring  
7. Lid Design  
   1. Must incorporate a light source that illuminates the sample to allow for clear imaging  
   2. Must allow for manual fluid input and output

   

### **Design Comparison** {#design-comparison}

![][image14]

##### **Figure 3.2 Risk Reduction Well Products** {#figure-3.2-risk-reduction-well-products}

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| WL.2: Watertight | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| WL. 4: Biocompatible | Yes | Yes, autoclavable | Yes | Yes, requires post-processing |

| Customization | Low | Moderate | Moderate | Yes |

| Requirement | Parallel Plates | Parallel Wires |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Field Uniformity | Extremely uniform | Poor, field concentrates near wires |

| Requirement | Titanium | Gold | Platinum |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

| Price (per gram) | $0.03 | $145 | $70 |

### **Final Design Justification** {#final-design-justification}

	The final chosen design for the well was 3D resin printing. This method maximizes customization while minimizing fabrication effort. This allows for the creation of internal geometries, such as the slots for the electrodes and the groove for the O-ring. Utilizing a square well design that opens to a circular lid allows the square body to house the electrodes while still incorporating 3D threads to secure the lid to the body to ensure a leak-proof assembly.  
	For the electric field generation component, parallel rectangular plates were selected as the optimal electrode configuration because they provide the most uniform electric field lines across the well and were most likely to resemble the Maxwell simulations. While the use of parallel wires would be easier to install and have a smaller physical footprint, they would have poor field uniformity as the field magnitude is greater closer to the wire. Titanium was chosen as the electrode material because it satisfies the biocompatibility and corrosion resistance requirements. It also serves as an inexpensive option compared to metals such as gold and platinum.

### **Fabrication Methods** {#fabrication-methods}

	Minimal physical fabrication was needed for the wells because the process of printing them involves uploading the CAD file to the Stratasys printer, then leaving it to print for an hour or two.   
	The electrodes were fabricated by cutting the titanium sheet to the appropriate dimensions and soldering copper wire to them to ground and charge the respective ground and positive electrode.

## ***Helmholtz Coil Electromagnet*** {#helmholtz-coil-electromagnet}

#### **![][image15]**

##### **Figure 3.3: Finished prototype Helmholtz coil with resin printed well, all dimensions accurate to the final version** {#figure-3.3:-finished-prototype-helmholtz-coil-with-resin-printed-well,-all-dimensions-accurate-to-the-final-version}

![][image16]

##### **Figure 3.4: CAD of finalized Helmholtz coil design and dimensions with well and hall effect PCB enclosed within.** {#figure-3.4:-cad-of-finalized-helmholtz-coil-design-and-dimensions-with-well-and-hall-effect-pcb-enclosed-within.}

![][image17]

##### **Figure 3.5 Electronics Pathway and Layout for the Helmholtz coil.** {#figure-3.5-electronics-pathway-and-layout-for-the-helmholtz-coil.}

	The magnetic stimulation subsystem utilizes a pair of AC/DC controllable Helmholtz coils designed to generate a uniform magnetic field between 0-5 mT across the entire well culture volume. As shown in figure 3.3 and 3.4, each coil is wound with 156 turns of 24 AWG magnet wire housed in a non-magnetic ASA 3D printed frame and driven by 2 custom PCBs which enable precise current regulation, waveform generation, and closed-loop field stabilization.

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-1}

1. Max field strength \> 5 mT at coil center.  
   1. Sufficient for measurable cellular response  
2. Spatial Uniformity has \< 5% deviation within the inner cylinder from coil face to face and across entire well culture volume.  
   1. Enables consistent simulation across all chambers  
3. Supports varied stimulation protocols and waveform generation  
   1. DC offset \+ AC modulation for square, sine, ramp, and step waves (0-250 Hz)  
   2. Allows for varied stimuli protocols static field vs dynamic cycling  
4. Thermally stable maximum temperature in the coils does not exceed safe handling limit of 75℃ during up to 7 days of operation  
   1. Prevents thermal stress on cell culture and harm to electronics or user

### 

### **Design Comparison** {#design-comparison-1}

###### **Table 3.4 Design Comparison for Magnetic Field Generator** {#table-3.4-design-comparison-for-magnetic-field-generator}

| Requirement | Helmholtz Coil | Horseshoe Magnet air gap |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| HM.1.1: Field Strength | 5.0 mT @ 1A, 156 turns of wire per coil. | 5.0 mT @ 0.5A, 120 turns of wire in 30mm winding space. |
| HM.2: Field Uniformity | Variance across the entire chamber from edge to edge of coils is \<1%. Easily predictable strength and uniformity from simple simulation largely align with theory. | Very low field variance across the Z axis, but across X and Y as much as 8% variance across the air gap between the well and the magnet. Hard to exactly predict the strength as it is very shape dependent and edge effects are hard to simulate. |
| MP.3: Waveform Generation | Easily integratable with a custom PCB system for control over both AC and DC fields using a waveform generator. Very low magnetic residuals and reluctance. | High reluctance of the system to field changing under AC and residual magnetism left over at 0A of current. |
| MP.4.1: Thermal Risk | Maximum heating is predicted to be \<40℃ increase, but needs to be tested. | Heating is very low due to the low current required to drive the system, resulting in a low rise in temperature. |
| MP.4.2: System Integration | Challenging form to integrate into the system required designing other components around the coils to fit into the system. | Relatively simple implementation of a 2d shape into design. |
| Price | \~$10 for coil \+ \~$30 per PCB | \~$50 for steel plus machining time, PCB cost unknown |

### **Final Design Justification** {#final-design-justification-1}

	Given the requirement for consistent stimulation across multiple chambers, the Helmholtz coil offers significantly superior uniformity reducing variables when evaluating cell response. In addition, Helmholtz coils allow for easier scalability as they have minimal cross talk between the systems at our current spacing. Most importantly, Helmholtz coils enable AC modulation and integrate easily with signals up to 250 Hz, compared to the significant reluctance of horseshoe magnets. In addition, after correcting an earlier error in coil spacing which had halved field strength, the coils are now thermally viable and will not need additional cooling hardware. Overall, while the horseshoe magnet offers a simpler design and better power efficiency, the Helmholtz coil’s exceptional field uniformity and experimental flexibility make it the perfect choice for this bioreactor application.

### **Fabrication Methods** {#fabrication-methods-1}

	The coil will be 3D printed out of ASA material, and then the coil will be wound by hand on a lathe, counting rotations in order to match the number of turns of wire between the two coils. Then, measuring both coils with a 4 wire configuration for a multimeter, resistances will be balanced by hand to within \<0.1 ohms to ensure consistent performance and uniformity. The PCB will be manufactured externally and mounted to the coil with M.2 screws.

	The microscope platform like the one shown in Fig 3.5 provides the interface between the microscope, which needs to follow individual cell cultures in the well, and the frame, which is static. The chosen 3-axis stage provides the range of motion necessary to obtain visually acceptable recordings throughout the duration of the test (as determined by the sponsor).

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-2}

1. Precision to track individual zebrafish embryo  
   1. The embryos are typically 700μm, so a \<100μm/count precision was requested  
2. Stability to hold the microscope without rocking or shaking in any perceptible manner  
3. Resistance to accidental knocks greater than \~300N of force  
4. Microscope positions are individually adjustable

### **Design Comparison** {#design-comparison-2}

###### **Table 3.5 Design Comparison for Microscope Platform** {#table-3.5-design-comparison-for-microscope-platform}

| Requirement | Pre-made 3-axis table | Custom leadscrew table | Custom belt drive |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| MP.1.1: Axis precision | \<10μm/tick, backlash-compensated | \<3.97μm/count, unknown backlash | \<80μm/count |
| MP.2: Stability | Yes | Yes | Requires correct tensions |
| MP.3: Impact Resistance | Theoretically infinite, stages have screw locks | \~675N braking force, practically infinite due to locking torque | \~90N |
| MP.4.1: Digital control | No | Yes | Yes |

| Price | $512.68 | \~$1000 | \~$800 |

### **Final Design Justification** {#final-design-justification-2}

	Originally, the plan was to use a large-format custom leadscrew table to move a carriage containing all four microscopes. However, late in development the sponsor clarified that he wished for all the microscopes to move independently. The labor required to make 4 consistent copies of a custom design was great, leading to consideration of modules that were fully assembled out of the box. The model that was eventually found utilized a near-identical motion system to our custom solution, using spring-loaded micrometers instead of ACME leadscrews and linear rails instead of rods, but otherwise retaining the same shape. The decision to use a leadscrew-based design in the first place is further detailed under the “Gantry System” individual component analysis in the appendix \[A.4, “Gantry System”\].  
	Overall, the premade 3-axis table meets every mandatory requirement at an equal or lower cost than a custom design, while also working straight out of the box and requiring no work on our part. Thus, it became the obvious choice.

### **Fabrication Methods** {#fabrication-methods-2}

	By design, no fabrication is required for this solution. M4 bolts are used to attach the table to a 3D-printed adapter to the microscope, as well as to the chassis structure underneath.

## ***Frame Mounting Plate*** {#frame-mounting-plate}

![][image20]

##### **Figure 3.7: CAD model of the upper plate of the MCCB. Large holes are clearance for the Helmholtz coils to fit through and the small holes surrounding them are mounting bolt holes. The electromagnets are attached from underneath the plate.** {#figure-3.7:-cad-model-of-the-upper-plate-of-the-mccb.-large-holes-are-clearance-for-the-helmholtz-coils-to-fit-through-and-the-small-holes-surrounding-them-are-mounting-bolt-holes.-the-electromagnets-are-attached-from-underneath-the-plate.}

	The frame mounting plate provides the platform by which all the biological and stimulus components come together. It is a CNC routed 9.525mm (⅜”) acetal plastic plate capable of receiving the well modules and bearing their weight while aligning them above the microscope modules.

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-3}

1. Provide stable structural support to the MCCB components, bearing the load without flexing  
   1. Plate flex less than 0.1mm under the full weight of the assembly  
2. Must prevent the generation of parasitic eddy currents in the area around the electromagnets  
3. Must be easily machinable to accommodate all the necessary features of the MCCB

### **Design Comparison** {#design-comparison-3}

###### **Table 3.6 Design Comparison for Microscope Platform** {#table-3.6-design-comparison-for-microscope-platform}

| Requirement | Acetal mounting plate | Austenitic (316) Stainless steel mounting plate | Aluminum Plate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| FP.1.1: Thickness required to meet stiffness requirement | 9.525mm (⅜”) thickness | 2.667mm (12 gauge, 0.105”) thickness | 3.175mm (⅛”) thickness |
| FP.2: Eddy current resistance | 0 current generation | Eddy current generated if cold-worked | High eddy current generation, requires splits |
| FP.3: Machinability | CNC Router, Waterjet, Laser cut | Waterjet, Laser cut | CNC Router, Laser cut, Waterjet,  |
| Price | $162.89 | $264.38 | $110.16 |

### **Final Design Justification** {#final-design-justification-3}

	Despite the aluminum plate being the ideal choice with regard to price and the 316 stainless steel having a thin profile, the presence of eddy currents posed such a large problem for the rest of the assembly that the Acetal plate became the best choice regardless. Eddy currents are induced circular electrical currents that are generated when conductive metal intersects a switching magnetic field, and it creates disturbances in the otherwise nearly perfectly uniform magnetic field generated by the Helmholtz coils. Eddy currents are also parasitic, in that they reduce the overall power of the electromagnet. Finally, eddy currents generate heat, which could be potentially antagonistic to the biological sample. Thus, the acetal plate was chosen and the rest of the components were adjusted around it. Other plastics were briefly considered, however Acetal is chemically inert, easy to machine, and the industry standard for stiff engineering plastic, so it was chosen over other plastics like acrylic or polypropylene.

## ***Optics Train*** {#optics-train}

# **![][image21]**

##### **Figure 3.8: The optics train assembly including an infinity corrected objective, extension tube set, and a USB FLIR camera module to image the sample.** {#figure-3.8:-the-optics-train-assembly-including-an-infinity-corrected-objective,-extension-tube-set,-and-a-usb-flir-camera-module-to-image-the-sample.}

	The microscope and camera assembly allows for observing the cells as well as capturing images of the observed sample throughout the duration of an experiment. The camera captures images of the sample either periodically or continuously over the duration of the experiment.  
	The modularity of the optics train assembly allows the user to easily replace parts to adjust the magnification and resolution capabilities. The infinity corrected objective lens selected allows for 20x magnification. A custom 3D printed ring was made to secure the tube lens inside the extension tube set. The focal length selection depends on the desired magnification and can be determined by the following equation:

(3.1)                                                     Mtotal \= FtubeFobjective

Where Ftube is the focal length of the tube lens and Fobjective is the focal length of the objective. Based on equation (3.1), it is expected that longer focal length tube lenses generally increase magnification, but also lead to a decreased field of view (FOV). Users may choose to swap lens lengths based on desired magnification and FOV requirements for each specific experiment.

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-4}

1. Have a long focal length to see deeper inside the sample (\~10mm)  
2. Have a camera that can record a video of the observed image  
3. The video should have a resolution capable of observing objects as small as 25μm

### **Design Comparison and Final Design Justification** {#design-comparison-and-final-design-justification}

The camera and entire microscope assembly was selected from parts that our sponsor already possessed in his lab. A custom 3d printed ring holder was made to secure the tube lens in the extension tube set.

![][image22]

##### **Figure 3.9: Reticle lens resolution and FOV imaging tests for the optics train assembly. Three focal length tube lenses were selected for testing.** {#figure-3.9:-reticle-lens-resolution-and-fov-imaging-tests-for-the-optics-train-assembly.-three-focal-length-tube-lenses-were-selected-for-testing.}

A reticle lens with tick mark divisions spaced 10 microns apart was used to test the resolution capabilities of the optics train assembly. Three focal length tube lens configurations (125mm, 100mm, and no tube lens) were selected for testing. Based on the images of the reticle lens, the no tube lens configuration appeared to provide the highest magnification and longer tube lens focal lengths appeared to decrease magnification. While these results are inconsistent with the magnification equation (3.1), it is possible that the custom 3D printed ring holder for the lens caused misalignment in the optics train leading to a decrease in magnification. For multichannel infinite-conjugate microscope assemblies, alignment is crucial as even slight tilt and off-center placement can result in a decrease in the magnification effect \[9\]. For future work, it is recommended that commercially available optics components are used without any custom made inserts as precision in the assembly and alignment is necessary for proper imaging. For the scope of this project, the team and sponsor agreed to proceed with the no tube lens configuration as the magnification and resolution was sufficient for initial testing of the prototype.  
![][image23]

##### **Figure 3.10: Particle found in fixed nucleus pulposus (NP) cell sample.** {#figure-3.10:-particle-found-in-fixed-nucleus-pulposus-(np)-cell-sample.}

	A fixed NP cell sample was placed in the wells and imaged with the optics train. While scanning the environment, it was unclear whether any cells were found as marks and spores in the resin printed lid often obstructed the view. However, a large unknown particle was detected in the sample. The particle was determined to be too round and large to be identified as an NP cell. For future imaging use, it is recommended that the resin lid either be blocked or printed with an optical grade biocompatible resin so that it does not obstruct the image view. 

## ***Central Electronics and User Interface*** {#central-electronics-and-user-interface}

The touchscreen user interface must be able to carry out the actions shown in figure 2.1 for the integrated MCCB system. The user must be able to apply individual electric and magnetic field intensities to each of the four wells. There must be closed loop monitoring from current sensors and hall sensors ensuring that the electric current and magnetic field stimuli do not exceed the safety limits which may lead to overheating and/or unintentional electrolysis to the cell cultures. In addition, the user must be able to view the camera displays under each well and be able to record and save images and data from each experiment session.  
![][image24]  
**Figure 3.11: Central Electronics System Diagram**

### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-5}

1. Independent well control  
   1. The UI shall allow the user to set individual electric and magnetic field parameters for each of the four wells independently, including field, magnitude and waveform type.  
   2. The UI shall allow the user to perform calibration on each individual well for precise control.  
2. Feedback Display  
   1. The UI shall display real-time readings from Hall effect sensors and current sensors for each well, confirming that the applied stimuli match commanded values and alerting the user if readings fall outside safe operating bounds.  
3. Camera viewing and capture  
   1. The UI shall display a live camera feed from each of the four microscope assemblies and allow the user to trigger image capture and recording.  
4. Accessible and responsive interface  
   1. The UI shall be operable entirely via touchscreen without requiring a keyboard or mouse and provide reliable use in a lab environment.

The primary risk areas for the integrated electronics include:

* Synchronization of imaging and stimuli application  
  - Solution: Use centralized control via Raspberry Pi  
* 4 cameras causing an overload risk  
  - Solutions:  
    - Powered 4 port USB hub  
    - Reduce acquisition load (eg. display lower FPS)  
* Power delivery requirements for multi-chamber stimulation   
  - Solution: External power supplies \+ centralized power distribution boards

As shown in figure 3.11, a master Raspberry Pi controller will be used to send commands to each Esp32 subsystem (electromagnet and electrode). The cameras will also be connected to the Raspberry Pi via a powered usb hub. To save recordings and data from experiments, the user can upload files to an external SSD Storage device.

When a user selects a stimulus mode, it first enters the gantry/camera calibration mode to align the camera using the manual gantry control and adjust the focus before beginning the experiment. Once the gantry is calibrated, the stimuli inputs are available as shown in figure 3.9 (c). The user can also choose when to capture images with the software by clicking the “record” button.

# **Chapter 4:‬ Prototype Performance** {#chapter-4:‬-prototype-performance}

## ***Electromagnet Prototype*** {#electromagnet-prototype}

### **Prototype Build** {#prototype-build}

![][image27]

##### **Figure 4.1 Breadboard setup with Helmholtz coil for testing.** {#figure-4.1-breadboard-setup-with-helmholtz-coil-for-testing.}

The prototype for the system consisted of a single piece 3D printed ASA Helmholtz coil wound with 24 AWG magnet wire with each coil having 156 turns at a 27mm radius and 27mm coil separation, consistent with the standard Helmholtz geometry. The breadboard setup integrates a Pololu 8876 H-Bridge driver and uses a Gaussmeter to measure performance. A variable bench power supply was used to drive the coil, limited to 1A in order to be consistent with the limitations of the driver in the final system.

**Performance**

The mechanical and electrical integration of the Helmholtz coil subsystem shows robust performance under initial testing and operation. The coil was fabricated using ASA plastic via 3D printing, selected for its thermal stability under the sustained heating from electromagnetic operation. Its integrated mounts successfully secured the cell culture well and satellite PCB together, ensuring compatibility. A power distribution board provides 24V input from the main power supply at currents up to 3A per well, with the control board for each well incorporating an ESP 32 with an H Bridge driver for AC operation of the wells. System calibration tests are used to balance the performance of the Hall effect sensor readings and correlate drive time percent operation values with their magnetic field strength output.

### **Design Verification and Validation** {#design-verification-and-validation}

#### **Theoretical:**

The theoretical magnetic field distribution for the Helmholtz coil configuration was derived using the standard analytical model for paired circular coils separated by a distance equal to their radius. Under ideal conditions, this geometry is predicted to yield a highly uniform magnetic field within the central region between the coils. The theoretical field strength Bt at the geometric center was calculated as: Bt=(45)3/20nIRwhere 0 is the permeability of free space, n is the number of turns per coil, I is the applied current, and R is the coil radius. Based on the finalized coil parameters, the predicted central field strength was 5 mT at a driving current of 1 A. The theoretical uniformity region was defined as the volume exhibiting ≤1% deviation from the center field value, extending radially to 25mm and axially to ±15mm from the coil midplane. Edge effects and minor winding imperfections were accounted for as variance in Python simulations, which predicted a gradual field decay at the outer boundary of the cell culture well footprint. 

#### **Coil Impedance Characterization:**

Prior to AC magnetic field testing, the electrical characteristics of the fabricated Helmholtz coil were measured using a NanoVNA vector network analyzer to determine safe operating frequency bounds and validate the coil’s impedance behaviour across the intended drive range.

![][image28]![][image29]

##### **Figure 4.2 Impedance (Siemens) magnitude vs Frequency (Hz) for 1kHz \-100kHz and Resistance and Reluctance vs Frequency (Hz) for 1kHz \-1mHz** {#figure-4.2-impedance-(siemens)-magnitude-vs-frequency-(hz)-for-1khz--100khz-and-resistance-and-reluctance-vs-frequency-(hz)-for-1khz--1mhz}

![][image30]![][image31]

##### **Figure 4.3 Inductance (H) vs Frequency (Hz) for 1kHz \-100kHz and Parasitic Capacitance (F) vs Frequency for 1kHz \-100kHz** {#figure-4.3-inductance-(h)-vs-frequency-(hz)-for-1khz--100khz-and-parasitic-capacitance-(f)-vs-frequency-for-1khz--100khz}

Figures 4.2 and 4.3 present the inductance, parasitic capacitance, impedance magnitude, and resistance / reactance measured between 1 kHz-1 MHz. The self-resonant frequency of the coil was identified to be at approximately 570 kHz, at which point parasitic capacitance and inductance cancel and the coil transitions from inductive to capacitive behaviour. To ensure purely inductive operation and avoid resonance driven instability, the maximum drive frequency was constrained to be no more than 1/10th of the self resonant frequency, placing the practical upper limit at approximately 57 kHz. The H-bridge driver (Pololu DRV8876) has a maximum PWM frequency of 20 kHz, which falls comfortably within this bound, confirming that the driver and coil are compatible across the full intended operating range of 0-250 Hz. 

Inductance measurements shown in Figure 4.3 stabilize at approximately 4.5 mH above 5 kHz, indicating consistent inductive behaviour well within the operating range. Parasitic capacitance decreases logarithmically from the low μF range at 1 kHz, to negligible nF levels above 5 kHz, confirming that the capacitive effects are insignificant at the relevant drive frequencies. Impedance as seen in Figure 4.2 is increasing linearly within our operating range which is consistent with inductance dominated behaviour where |Z|=L. These results confirm that the coil is acting like a pure inductor through the 0-250 Hz operating window, and that no derating or frequency dependent compensation is required within this range.

#### **Test Conditions:**

Magnetic field characterization was conducted carefully to ensure isolation of coil performance from environmental interference. To do this a precision magnetometer was used and calibrated to 0 accounting for the presence of Earth’s magnetic field and any residual magnetic fields in the lab. The coil was then powered by a lab bench and current limited to exactly 1A. Measurements were taken at an array of points in the X, Y and Z directions in order to capture any potential edge effects. The results have been radially interpolated and displayed in Figure 4.2.  
![][image32]

##### **Figure 4.4 Theoretical and experimental magnetic field values within the inner region of the Helmholtz coil.** {#figure-4.4-theoretical-and-experimental-magnetic-field-values-within-the-inner-region-of-the-helmholtz-coil.}

#### **Results:**

The experimental measurements strongly agreed with theoretical predictions across the testing region. The measured surface field closely tracked the model with a peak central reading of 4.98 mT under normal operating conditions. Field intensity exhibited a gradual radial decay, with values dropping to 4.67 mT at the inner radius of the coils, and sharply from the inner radius outwards after that. As anticipated, the field drop was significant compared to the theoretical due to the winding thickness and housing constraints. Spatial mapping of the results above however, show that the entirety of the well’s footprint lies within the 99% uniformity contour which has a maximum field deviation of \<1% relative to the center point. Axial characterization shows minimal variation in the region between the two faces of the coils. In addition, further AC testing confirmed the ability of the coils to reach 5mT with 24V driving current under 1A between 0-250 Hz upper limit. Thermal testing was performed showing a rise of up to 80 degrees Celsius on the motor driver and 65 degrees Celsius on the coils after 2 hours of operation at 5 mT square waves at 100 Hz.

![][image33]

##### **Figure 4.5 Field readings from Hall Effect sensors for square waves at 100 Hz.** {#figure-4.5-field-readings-from-hall-effect-sensors-for-square-waves-at-100-hz.}

As seen above, Figure 4.5 shows the readings from the satellite PCB hall effect sensors during square wave operation at 100 Hz. This validates both the PWM control system’s ability to generate the target field and the two sensor’s ability to track the changes in real time. The sensor output shows it following the waveform and also the time taken for the coil to actually induce the field as shown by the curves on the rise and fall times. From this we can see how the switching is consistent, with the readings looking very similar and there is very low overshoot or undershoot for this system. These all indicate the stable driveability of this system and its effective characterization from the Hall effect readings.

## ***Electrode Prototype*** {#electrode-prototype}

### **Prototype Build** {#prototype-build-1}

To test the electrode, a 5V power supply was connected to a Pololu DRV8876 motor driver, and its output was connected to the two electrode plates via the proposed ring terminal crimps. An ESP32 sent sine wave PWM commands to the driver, and an oscilloscope with alligator clips was used to probe the titanium plate itself.

### **Performance** {#performance}

	To verify the performance of the electrode PWM control reliability, a dry environment validation test was performed. For the dry environment test, a 100 load resistor was placed as a stand-in for the saline solution as shown in Figure 4.6. The 100 value was selected because it approximates the resistance of saline solution (68/cm) across a 1.4cm for a total resistance of 95.2. Throughout the dry environment testing, various input voltages were tested and verified based on current draw measurements from an INA219 sensor as well as direct measurements of the load voltage at the electrodes using a multimeter. These results were further verified by comparing to theoretical values based on Ohm’s Law V=IR. The PWM control parameters were calibrated until the measured current and voltage values were consistent with input voltage. Once the dry environment control calibration was complete, the same experiments were performed inside the wells filled with saline solution. Overall, the tests indicated reliable control via PWM to achieve the expected voltage load consistently (Figure 4.7).

# **Chapter 5: Design Recommendations and Conclusions** {#chapter-5:-design-recommendations-and-conclusions}

## ***Conclusion*** {#conclusion}

The Multi-Chamber-Camera Bioreactor was developed to provide Dr. Chen with a research platform for studying the effects of electric and magnetic field stimulation on stem cell differentiation. The final design delivers four independently controllable well assemblies with VeroClear resin-printed chambers, titanium plate electrodes, sealed fluid ports, and optically clear imaging windows, unified together with a touchscreen interface running on a central Raspberry Pi and ESP32 control architecture. 

The subsystems of this design work together to apply desired stimulation. The Helmholtz coil works to achieve peak fields of more than 5 mT which is within 0.4% of the theoretical prediction, and there is less than 1% spatial deviation across the entire well footprint and validated AC operation from 0-250 Hz. The electric field subsystem successfully drives all wave types through the plates between 0-100 Hz, and stays with a lower 5V input voltage in order to prevent electrolysis in the well as well as staying below 1.5 V/cm. The optics train is able to deliver precise magnification and resolution sufficient for the imaging of the desired cells and is able to be uniquely positioned on a three axis stage. Finally, the user interface is able to communicate with and control all the subsystems while providing the interaction point for the researchers delivering clear results and allowing precise control.

Not all deliverables were able to reach the desired full integration within the project timeline. The custom drive PCB was not successfully revised in time and the system currently operates on perf board assemblies, and cross well magnetic isolation needs to be formally characterized. These are the primary followup items, but despite this the MCCB delivers a functional, characterized, and well documented platform whose modular architecture allows individual subsystems to be iterated upon without a full system redesign. Delivering Dr. Chen with a capable foundation for stem cell stimulation research.

## ***Next Steps*** {#next-steps}

The intention of this apparatus was not to create a mass-producible product, but to provide a highly specialized apparatus to facilitate this specific branch of stem cell design. There is no future plan to adjust the design to be mass-produced but improvements upon this design are included in the following Recommendations section.

## ***Recommendations*** {#recommendations}

* The 3030 aluminum t-slot extrusion chassis is an ad hoc solution for a sturdy frame and rapid, adjustable prototyping. In the future, waterjet sheet metal with tapped fasteners is a much more dimensionally stable and square assembly method.  
* The Stratasys Veroclear resin actually has a biocompatible version created expressly for this kind of application. If a new/dedicated machine is available or the user is willing to flush the previous incompatible resin out of the machine, using this resin will prevent the need for the sodium hydroxide bath and will eliminate the risk of resin deeper in the part leaching into the sample and toxifying it  
* Plating the titanium electrodes with platinum is industry standard to prevent corrosion and the buildup of a resistive titanium oxide layer  
* The current final version uses components mounted on perf boards to drive the magnetic and electric fields. A PCB was intended to be used, but issues with the board and not having the time for a revision lead us to the decision to scrap it for now. For a final version, an updated version of the PCB is recommended to be used to drive the magnetic and electric fields, this should reduce the footprint of the device and introduce more robust and stable control systems for the magnetic and electrical fields.

## ***Applicable Standards*** {#applicable-standards}

* Optics  
  * The ISO 12233 standard will be used for image resolution and clarity testing, determining the MTF of the entire imaging stack. An eSFR target will be used for this test.  
* Well Leakage  
  * Bioreactor chambers must pass the bubble emission leakage test detailed in ASTM E515 and hydrostatic pressure test detailed in ASTM E1003-13(2022)  
    * A well can be filled past the brim in many situations for the entire duration of the test, and this will ensure that it will not leak by any significant amount during that time.  
* Safety of electrical systems  
  * Due to the presence of exposed electrical components, the requirements detailed in IEC 61010-1 will be followed. The vast majority of these are already met by committing to SELV, with lower than 50V AC and 120V DC voltage maximums enforced throughout the design.  
  * Per the guidelines, any electronic components potentially exposed to saline spills will be IP65 water-resistant or above.  
* Sustainable Development, Environmentally Friendly Design, and Global Conformity  
  * Due to the small scale and scope of the project, investment into sustainable development, environmentally friendly processes, and global conformity will be minimal. However, if this instrument were to be scaled and distributed, that process would follow ISO 14001, ISO 14006, and ISO 17000 Series guidelines, respectively.  
* Biocompatibility  
  * Since the wells are custom made from 3D-Printed Veroclear resin, the wells must be sterilizable and biocompatible for cell culture studies. The Veroclear material aligns with ISO 10993-1:2018 standards for biological evaluation of medical devices. The sterile properties of Veroclear resin can be strengthened through treatment with a sodium hydroxide/sodium metasilicate solution as detailed in \[[reference \#](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9018575/)\].  
  * To attach the optical cover glass slides to the wells, a medical grade adhesive must be used. Loctite AA 3979 UV cure adhesive gel follows ISO-10993, meaning it is biocompatible for medical device standards which align with the ISO 14971 risk-management process.

## ***Impact on Society*** {#impact-on-society}

This project creates a tool for bioengineers to perform experiments to make discoveries regarding the impact of electric and magnetic fields on cells. As the design engineers it is important for our team to consider the life cycle use of the product and its impact on society. While engineers have made significant technological contributions to society, it is part of their role to consider how their technology will affect mankind and the environment. Here are some key categories pertaining to this project’s Impact on Society:

* Increased accessibility to bioengineering research tools  
  This project will be able to provide a more cost-effective option to controlled cell environments. By developing a reproducible, cost-effective bioreactor system with customizability and a user-friendly interface for setting experimental parameters, this project lowers the barrier to researchers. This allows a broader range of scientists to contribute to the field of electrobiology.  
* Expansion of cell differentiation research  
  This project is intended to be used to observe the effect of magnetic and electric field stimuli on stem cells. This research on cell differentiation will explore different avenues for controlling stem cell differentiation research which could be impactful in the broader field of regenerative medicine. 

## ***Professional Responsibility*** {#professional-responsibility}

Within the scope of the project the team has aimed to align the design and implementation of the bioreactor with the team’s technical capabilities and its intended use in a research laboratory environment. The team has taken care to ensure that the device operates within validated operating conditions with respect to electrical and magnetic stimulation, thermal constraints, and fluid handling. Design decisions were made with consideration to reliable implementation and without introducing unnecessary risk to biological samples or users.  
Given the system’s use as a biomedical instrument, focus has turned to safe use in the laboratory and contamination risks. Electrical components were chosen to ensure safe compatibility with cell cultures and thermal constraints were made with consideration to biological sensitivity to prevent possible cell culture damage. This product is only intended for fabrication and use at a single laboratory, as such while the team has focused on adhering to standard laboratory practices when possible, this instrument is not intended for widespread medical use.  
In the collection of data and creation of functional parameters the team has maintained a commitment to honesty and clarity. All listed results and parameters are presented objectively with acknowledgement of limitations and with our utmost commitment to accurate and practical interpretation. The team has maintained regular coordination and meetings with our Sponsor to ensure the product aligns with expectations. Documentation of design decisions and revisions has been maintained to allow for reproducibility and understanding.  
The team recognizes that stem cell research is at the cutting edge of medical technologies and has broad implications. While the focus is on controlled academic testing, the project has been approached with ethical consideration focused on responsible use, transparency in documentation, and the importance of responsible development in emerging biomedical technologies for the betterment of humanity.

### **Risk Reduction Effort** 

#### **Well Design and Fabrication**

The wells are a critical component of the MCCB as they must be biocompatible, sterilizable, hold fluids without leaking, compatible with microscope imaging from the bottom, allow users to insert and remove fluids, and not interfere significantly with stimuli applied to the cell culture samples as noted in the first section of the functional requirements. Three fabrication approaches with 3D printed VeroClear resin, machined delrin, and adapted off-the-market polypropylene plastic jars were manufactured and tested alongside both screw top and bolted clamp lid sealing methods were explored. To identify the most reliable method for the well design and fabrication, each approach was manufactured and characterized based on lead time, operational risks, and ability to hold fluid pressure.

Based on results from characterization tests measuring liquid leak over time, air pressure drop over time, and operational repeatability evaluation, the VeroClear resin 3D printed design with a screw top lid and an o-ring seal was selected. The VeroClear resin was determined to be the most customizable design with the fastest lead time while also showing promising results with zero measurable liquid loss over time and only a 0.46 psi drop from an initial 10 psi pressure over ten minutes. There was also no significant operational risk identified in the screw-top lid with an o-ring seal. The technical and operational risks followed by the selection process for the well design pathway is summarized below.

![][image40]

For microscope imaging from the bottom, an optical grade glass cover slide was secured to the bottom of each well with medical grade Loctite 3979 UV cure glue. No signs of leaking or damage were observed across all four design pathways and characterization tests.

#### **Optical Clarity and Imaging Capability**

As listed in functional requirements 1.1.1 and 1.1.2, the well bottom shall be constructed of a material that has \>95% light transmission and \< 2% haze and have a thickness less than the focal length of the microscope (\< 5 mm). In addition, the optical instruments must follow the requirements listed in section 2 of the functional requirements to provide magnification for resolution to image zebrafish embryo which are approximately 25 micrometers in diameter and provide proper illumination with either white light or 550 nm green light integrated with a diffuser. 

Once the camera and microscope assembly are selected and confirmed with our sponsor, characterization tests will be performed by imaging the USAF 1951 resolution chart shown in Fig. XX below to verify that the optical assembly can properly image at the zebrafish embryo scale.  
![][image45]

###### **Figure A.1.2 \- USAF 1951 Resolution Chart** {#figure-a.1.2---usaf-1951-resolution-chart}

#### **Magnetic Field Generation**

To achieve the magnetic field generation requirements listed in section 3 of the functional requirements, an air gap horseshoe magnet and Helmholtz coil were designed and tested for uniformity with magnetometer and inductance measurements as discussed further in the Chapter 4 Performance section.

#### **Electric Field Stimulation**

To achieve the electric field stimulation requirements listed in section 4 of the functional requirements, simulations were run to predict electric field uniformity between two titanium plate electrodes across a saline solution. To avoid unintended electrolysis from occurring due to current being too high, current sensors will be integrated in the final system to monitor the current going through the electrodes.
