## ***A.4 Designs Considered***

### **2-Axis Gantry Solutions** {#2-axis-gantry-solutions}

One of the earlier design requirements for this project was for the camera and microscope module to be movable in 2 axes across the viewing window of the well. The requirement was that it must be stable and have fine control, and calls for a precise 2-3D gantry system below each microscope. This part of the design has since been removed as the team chose for manual adjustment of the microscope via a linear stage, but the discussion for the initial considerations for incorporation into the design is still included in the following section.  
Precise linear movement is a problem that has been solved many times over, namely in the field of autonomous manufacturing. CNC Machines require high precision under high load due to the cutting forces required for harder materials. Thus, most mills and routers use leadscrews to achieve linear motion, which are incredibly resistant to backdriving and have very high torque conversion, as well as a heavy gear down ratio to allow for precision under both automated and manual operation \[6\].  
	Alternatively, 3d printers have a much higher demand for speed over torque, and thus use belt drives for both horizontal axes (example pictured in figure 2). This allows for agile motion while having sufficient precision from GT2 belts and standard microstepping technology, with the tradeoff being the need for tensioners on each belt and a massive deflection under load. The precision ceiling for belt drives is also lower than leadscrews, however it does not suffer from as much backlash.

![][image46]

##### **Figure A.4.1: Belt driven 3-axis gantry designed by Dylan Lee, 2024** {#figure-a.4.1:-belt-driven-3-axis-gantry-designed-by-dylan-lee,-2024}

### **Individual Component Analysis** {#individual-component-analysis}

#### **Lid Design (by Dylan Bailes)**

Project Description:  
	The focus of the project is to develop a complete multi-chambered lab testing equipment to determine the impact of certain stimuli on the growth of cell samples. To complete this objective we must develop implementation for the key stimuli: magnetic fields and electric fields, while allowing for the clear imagining of these wells from below. The wells are 20mm in diameter and are where the cells are contained. The lid serves to provide a seal for the well, and an interface between the external stimuli hardware and the cells inside the well. In order to do this the lid must satisfy several requirements. All ports in and out of the well must form a watertight seal ensuring that no fluid leaks from the cell during operation. It must include ports for fluid input and outlet to allow for the exchange of fluid during the tests. Secondly, it must provide access ports for electrodes to be inserted across the well which will then provide a controlled electric field to the well. In addition, the individual external magnetic field stimuli must have room to be integrated into the system around the well and the lid must enable this, holding the magnetic field in place without interfering with the generation or character of the field. Lastly, all of the ports must be able to fit in the 20mm diameter footprint of the lid covering the top of the well.

Functional Requirements:

1. Fluid Transfer System  
   1. The lid shall provide at least one fluid inlet port into the well.  
   2. The lid shall provide at least one fluid outlet port from the well.  
   3. The inlet and outlet ports should allow for controlled fluid exchange from the well with minimum flow rate of 100 mL/min.  
   4. All fluid ports and seals shall maintain a watertight seal with zero visible leakage for a minimum period of 48 hours.  
2. Electrical Stimulation System  
   1. The lid shall provide access points for insertion and powering of two electrodes into the well.  
   2. The access points shall maintain a watertight sealed interface around the electrodes, with zero fluid leakage at operating conditions.  
   3. The electrodes shall be positioned such that a controlled electric field can be generated across the cell culture.  
3. Magnetic Field Accomodation  
   1. The lid shall allow the incorporation of a magnetic field source across the well.  
   2. The lid shall be constructed from materials with a relative magnetic permeability of r1.05 to avoid distortion of the applied magnetic field.  
4. Compatibility and Integration  
   1. The lid shall attach and detach from the well without causing any damage to the well.  
   2. The lid shall maintain uniform compression of sealing elements across the sealing surface with a minimum force of 120N.  
   3. The lid shall withstand expected mechanical loads during operation, with deflection of less than 0.25 mm.  
   4. The lid shall allow for repeatable sealing of more than 100 cycles without degradation in sealing performance.  
   5. The lid shall have consistent alignment with the well to within \+- 0.1mm in the X and Y axes.  
   6. All materials shall be compatible with the cell culture and not introduce any unwanted external effects.

Component Options:  
System 1 \- Adhesive Bonded, Delrin Lid (Low complexity)  
All seals are formed by applying a bio compatible medical grade silicone adhesive to holes machined into a Delrin lid. The fluid and electrode port access is done by directly applying this adhesive to the electrodes and fluid tubing. This approach does not require any precise machining and uses simple parts, but may not be the best for long term repair and operating considerations for leak proof performance.

| Sub-Component | Technical Considerations |
| :---- | :---- |
| Electrode Port | Sealant Type: Permatex 80050 Clear Silicone Adhesive Sealing:  Adhesive applied directly to electrodes or heatshrink. Watertight when static. Silicone adhesive provides no active sealing force on the electrode, electrode movement during operation can open a leak path, which may violate the zero leakage requirement. Can not repair the seal easily without replacing it completely. Compatibility: Compatible with 8-36 AWG wire; platinum, copper and titanium all compatible Silicone is diamagnetic r1 Lead Time and Costs: 24 hr curing time $6 per 3oz (approx. $0.12 per port) Available immediately from Home Depot for pickup |
| Fluid Port | Sealant Type: Permatex 80050 Clear Silicone Adhesive Sealing: Adhesive applied around tubing. Watertight when static. Silicone adhesive provides no active sealing force on the tubing, tubing movement during operation can open a leak path, which may violate the zero leakage requirement. Can not repair the seal easily without replacing it completely. Compatibility: Bonds to silicone tubing and PVC tubing well. Does not bond to Polyurethane, PTFE, PFA, Polyethylene or Polypropylene tubing. Silicone is diamagnetic r1 Lead Time and Costs: 24 hr curing time $6 per 3oz (approx. $0.12 per port) Available immediately from Home Depot for pickup |
| Lid Material | Material: Delrin (Polyoxymethylene) Plate Processing: CNC milling from plate to incorporate wells and ports. Can be done with standard tools very simple to machine. Tolerance of \+- 0.1mm is very doable to achieve through CNC milling. Material Info and Compatibility: Young’s modulus: 3.1 GPa, this is sufficient for deflection under 120N load across 20mm disk at 5mm thickness is \< 0.05mm, meets \< 0.25mm requirement. Fully non magnetic r=1 Delrin is Biocompatible Doesn’t bond well with silicone adhesives, needs to be sanded or primed first. Taps well for threaded fitting holes. Cost and Lead Time: $89.50 for a 12” x 12” x 0.5” 2 day lead time on Mc Master other sources exist for cheaper but lead time increases. |

System 2 \- Compression Fitting, Barbed Port, Acrylic Lid (Medium complexity)  
This system uses a machined acrylic lid top with threaded interfaces for fluid and electrode access. Electrode Sealing is done through a brass compression fitting that provides a mechanical seal around the electrode rod. Fluid ports are done through 1/16-27 NPT Nylon barbed fluid fittings designed for microfluidics tubing. This needs precise threaded interfaces and CNC machining and provides a more accurate and stiffer seal than System 1\.

| Sub-Component | Technical Considerations |
| :---- | :---- |
| Electrode Port | Fitting Type: Brass Compression Fitting to grip the electrode rod Sealing:  The ferrule deforms around the rod as the nut tightens forming a radial compression seal. Seal is leak free when correctly torqued to manufacturer specifications. Requires consistent tightening torque as over or under tightening can compromise seal performance which induces leaks. Holds a dynamic sealing force on the rod. Rated for \>50 cycles for compression fitting before ferrule deformation endangers seal. Repairable by replacing the compression fitting simply. Compatibility: Electrode rod size 0.125” OD, standard electrode rod stock but less free form than silicone seal. Brass is not biocompatible and not ideal for direct cell contact. The electrode rod should be platinum or titanium. Brass is non-ferromagnetic r1 Lead Time and Costs: $3.43 (50815K102 Mc Master Carr) per fitting 2 days |
| Fluid Port | Fitting Type: Nylon barbed tube fitting (1/16” barb, threaded body) Sealing: Threads into tapped holes in the acrylic lid. PTFE tape applied to the threads for additional sealing and leak resistance. Barbed fitting is leak free under static low flow conditions, flow is about 100 mL/min through 1/16” ID tubing so low flow applies. Holds a mechanical grip on the tubing OD more robust than simple adhesion bonding in system 1\. Barb is susceptible to loosen under vibration or repeated tubing removal. Needs to be checked and possibly replaced occasionally. Compatibility: Nylon has biocompatible options available and non magnetic, r=1. Replaceable as fittings can be unscrewed and replaced into the same lid with new PTFE tape. Lead Time and Costs: $0.17 each for 100 Lead time: 2 weeks |
| Lid Material | Material: Acrylic Plate Processing: CNC milling from plate to incorporate wells and threads precisely. Achievable tolerance of \+-0.1mm Material Info and Compatibility: Young’s modulus: 2.4-3.3 GPa, provides adequate stiffness, \<0.05mm deflection for 120N load across a 20mm disk at 5mm thickness Fully non magnetic r=1 Acrylic is biocompatible Risk of brittle fracture as acrylic is sensitive to sharp corners and stress fractures can occur from over tightening. Bonds decently with silicone adhesives. Tapped threads can be brittle and break Bonds well to silicone glues. Lead Time and Costs: $37.78 for a 12” x 12” x 0.5” sheet 2 day lead time |

System 3 \- Spring Energized Seal, Luer Lock, PEEK Lid (Highest complexity)  
This system uses a PEEK (Polyether Ether Ketone) machined lid, with a spring energized PTFE lip seal for electrode access and a 10-32 UNF Luer lock adapter for fluid ports. The spring energized seal is self sealing, maintaining continuous radial contact on the electrode even if it moves about slightly. The Luer lock serves as a standard microfluidics connector that can withstand repeated connections and disconnects. This system offers a robust seal with a long cycling lifetime but introduces greater manufacturing and component complexity.

| Sub-Component | Technical Considerations |
| :---- | :---- |
| Electrode Port | Fitting Type: Spring Energized PTFE seal with 316 stainless steel coil spring  Spring maintains continuous radial force on the electrode rod, maintaining a leak free and self sealing design even during rod movement. Designed for continuous sealing and compression \>100 cycles Repairable by replacing the compression fitting simply. Tapered OD for a tight seal in the hole, but needs to be precisely inserted into countersunk bore for effective interference fit. Compatibility: Electrode rod size 0.125” OD, standard electrode rod stock but needs to be precisely ground radially for effective sealing which adds risk and complexity. Brass is not biocompatible and not ideal for direct cell contact. The electrode rod should be platinum or titanium. PTFE r1, Stainless Steel spring r1.006, within r1.05. 3/16” OD fits comfortably within 20mm diameter well Lead Time and Costs: $26.12 (50815K102 Mc Master Carr) per fitting 3 days |
| Fluid Port | Fitting Type: 10-32 UNF to Female Luer lock adapter Sealing: Threads into 10-32 tapped holes in the PEEK lid. PTFE tape applied to the threads for additional sealing and leak resistance. Designed for PTFE and silicone microfluidics tubing, standard lock connector makes it easy to switch tubing when needed. Luer lock thread engagement provides a leak free connection when fully attached needs to be tightened to appropriate torque. Risk as it depends on correct thread engagement. Compatibility: Polypropylene is biocompatible and r=1. Luer locks are available in lab grade. Replaceable as fittings can be unscrewed and replaced into the same lid with new PTFE tape. Luer OD is 9mm harder to package but doable within 20mm spacing. Luer ID is about 2.5mm which can easily meet 100 mL/min requirement. Lead Time and Costs:  $52.53 per 25 Luer locks ($2.10 each)  Lead time: 5 days |
| Lid Material | Material: PEEK (Polyether Ether Ketone) Processing: CNC milling from plate to incorporate wells and threads and bores. Achievable tolerance of \+-0.1mm Material Info and Compatibility: Young’s modulus: 3.6 GPa, highest stiffness of the options, \<0.02mm deflection for 120N load across a 20mm disk at 5mm thickness, exceeds requirement. Purely diamagnetic r=1. USP Class VI / ISO 10993 certified the highest biocompatibility rating, ideal for use in medical devices. Can be autoclaved. Very high mechanical properties make it ideal for holding repeatedly even under many cycles. bond well with silicone adhesives, needs to be sanded or primed first. Tapped threads can be brittle and break Bonds poorly to silicone glues. Lead Time and Costs: $517.99 for a 12” x 12” x 0.5” sheet is very expensive, consider blending with other materials to use less. 10 day lead time takes a while. |

Design Recommendation and Rationale:  
Best System: System 2  
This system combines the important aspects of keeping to something that is easy to use, implement, and replace, while still meeting all needed requirements for the task.  
The compression fitting provides an effective and reliable way for repeated engagement of the copper rod and sealing at a low cost. Comparatively, system 1 gives a sealing method that while functional for a prototype is not robust under the end goal of turning this into a long term use piece of laboratory equipment. In addition, while system 3 also provides an effective way to seal the electrodes with no leakage, it requires a more precise counter bore and interference fit which is not the simplest to machine and integrate as well as it costs significantly more for the spring energized seals.  
For fluid fittings System 2 also gives a very effective solution as a barbed fitting and threaded port is a robust and simple system which should hold an effective leak free seal given the simplicity of the flow in our system. This is a closer determination though as system 3 also has a compelling option of Luer Locks, but ultimately it came down to packaging constraints as while they both provide effective sealing methods the Luer Lock OD being 9mm makes it much harder to fit into the well lid as two of them plus the electrode ports will be far harder to work with than the 6mm for the barbed fittings. System 1 on the other hand does give a quick way to get a leak free seal that can be done simply and doesn’t need any external components or machining, but it also fixes itself to the lid making it very challenging to make any repairs or modifications to the system without replacing the lid in its entirety.  
Lastly, material wise System 2 with acrylic is an effective option as it is far cheaper than the other two options of PEEK and Delrin while filling all of the same requirements. All the materials, PEEK, Delrin and acrylic are sufficient under the applied force to the lid to remain stiff enough, as well as they are all biocompatible materials. While PEEK may perform slightly stiffer and is the gold standard for medical engineering materials, it also is priced like gold to cost more than 10x what the acrylic costs. As such while it is an effective engineering material it is also not within our budget.   
Overall I would rank System 2, then System 3, and finally System 1\. Based on these above reasons I believe that System 2 is the best path forward to proceed with as it meets all the needs specified in the functional requirements for the system while not going out of its way to increase the technical and financial burden associated with integrating such a system. System 3 increases the technical burden of the project adding in additional layers of precision which risk this project's timely completion, while System 1 fails to meet the requirements to provide robust and repairable sealing options. As such System 2 is my recommendation going forward.

Project Description:

This project involves the design of a custom lid for a single-well cell culture system, intended to apply multiple simultaneous stimuli to biological cells grown in vitro. The well is a 20mm diameter cylindrical culture vessel in which cells are seeded and maintained under controlled conditions. The lid is a critical subsystem of this device — it serves as the primary interface between the external stimulation hardware and the cells inside the well, meaning that every form of stimulus and every fluid interaction with the culture must pass through or be enabled by the lid.

The device is designed to expose cultured cells to combined mechanical, electrical, and/or magnetic stimuli in order to study their physiological responses. To support this, the lid must satisfy several functional requirements. First, it must include dedicated ports for fluid input and fluid removal, allowing cell culture media to be replenished and samples to be extracted without disturbing the culture. Second, it must provide access positions for electrodes to be inserted across the well, enabling a controlled electric field to be applied to the cells. Third, the geometry of the lid must accommodate the passage of a magnetic field through the well. All of these features must be integrated within the 20mm diameter footprint of the lid.

A key constraint across all lid features is that every port and access point must form a watertight seal, ensuring that no cell culture media leaks from the well during operation. This is essential both for maintaining the sterile culture environment and for ensuring consistent, repeatable experimental conditions.

Pressure Generation (Optional) 1\. The lid shall allow pressurization of the well interior. 2\. The lid shall maintain structural integrity under the maximum well pressure of 3 Atms. 3\. The lid shall allow for repeatable sealing \>100 cycles. 5\. The lid shall have consistent alignment with the well. 6\. #### **User Interface and Electronics System Integration (by Kaitlyn Lavarias)**

Overview  
The Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor’s (MCCB) goal is to use a gantry-microscope system to image the behavior of multiple cell culture samples under different stimuli such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and hydrostatic pressure as shown in Figure 1\. The user interface (UI) must be able to provide control over the stimuli inputs as well as allow for 2 DOF control of the gantry-miscroscope system. The user interface must organize and display photo/video captured from each chamber and record the input stimuli conditions. There are also safety concerns regarding multiple electronic components surrounding cell chamber holding fluid solutions, the risk of unintended electrolysis of cells if voltage applied is too high, and magnetic fields generated over long periods of time causing electromagnets to overheat \[1\]. The UI and sensors ultimately must work together to provide intuitive control for the user, have safety constraints over system control based on sensor readings, and organize images with corresponding stimuli conditions in each chamber.  
![][image47]  
Figure 1\. Integrated system showing the stimulus modes the user can select for the MCCB, the gantry and imaging controls, as well as the sensors on the hardware system (thermistors, pressure sensors, and hall sensors) necessary for ensuring safety of the electronics system and preventing damage to cell cultures.

Functional Requirements

1. Allow for 2-5V/cm input to cell cultures via electrodes in the cell chambers  
   1. Safety Constraint: voltage too high will cause unintended electrolysis to occur  
      1. User interface must cap the possible input limit at 5V/cm, outputting a safety error if input exceeds 5V/cm.  
2. Need to be able to apply up to 15 Gauss magnetic field strength  
   1. Safety Constraint: to generate a continuous magnetic field over several hours, there is a risk for the electromagnets to overheat  
      1. Integrated electronics must include thermistor sensors on the coils to detect overheating (must remain below 50 degrees Celsius) and hall sensors to ensure that the actual magnetic field strength is in the safe range (0 to 15 Gauss) \[2\], \[3\].  
3. Allow for insertion of fluidic cell culture samples into cell chambers \- house electronics away from fluidic chambers  
   1. Safety constraint: leaking fluids can damage electronics   
      1. Integrated electronics include pressure sensors which detect pressure drops (0.1 atm/sec) from the initial experiment conditions to detect leaks. Operations paused and warning displayed on UI.  
4. Allow for control of 2 DOF linear translation of the gantry system  
   1. Functional Constraint: Between swapping cell cultures and stimuli modes, the camera positioning and focus will likely be inconsistent.  
      1. User interface must include a calibration mode for the camera to ensure that the camera position for each chamber is focused before proceeding with stimuli experiments. The system is precalibrated with x-y coordinates of the center for each chamber (eg. chamber 1 located at x=30mm, y=30mm). The user can adjust these coordinates between experiments.  
5. Must save and organize the images of each cell culture chamber with the corresponding recorded input stimulus  
   1. Functional Constraint: With 4 chambers, there can be an overwhelming amount of information from sensor readings and images, so the images and data must be clearly organized for user readability.  
      1. UI: When done recording, automatically save a data sheet txt file of the sensor recordings labeled in columns. Each image is automatically labeled with time stamps and uploaded to a file labeled with corresponding chamber number. 

User Interface Options:  
The primary consideration for the UI is whether it will be controlled through an external device connection or a built in interface with the MCCB.

1. Software program on external computer

![][image48]  
![][image49]  
Figure 2\. Computer software interface showing the home page (a), the gantry/camera calibration (b), the magnetic field generation stimulus mode (c), and warning screen when a safety error is detected by sensors on the electronics system (d)

1. Function: The MCCB connects to an external laptop or computer through a USB connection which is controlled through an ESP32 microcontroller. The external computer would run a software interface used to control the stimuli inputs (electric field, magnetic field, hydrostatic pressure) as well as gantry motion. The microcontroller and wires are housed on the top of the well base away from the fluidic chambers housed below the well base. Since the electrode wires must be placed through a hole to the chambers, the hole must be coated with silicone to prevent leaks to the electronics above \[1\].  
   1. UI starts at the home screen as shown in Figure 2(a) where the user can find information about the MCCB use and specifications in the top tabs and choose a stimulus mode experiment mode to enter. When a user selects a stimulus mode, it first enters the gantry/camera translation calibration mode to set chamber coordinates and ensure proper camera focus as shown in Figure 2(b). Once the gantry is calibrated, the stimuli inputs are available as shown in Figure 2(c). The user can also choose when to capture images with the software by clicking the “record” button.  
   2. Safety: The software will have built in safety constraints for a set maximum value of stimuli intensity as well as a maximum speed setting for gantry translation. In addition, the thermistor and pressure sensors on the MCCB will communicate with the UI if there are dangerous conditions approaching overheating, unintended electrolysis, and/or and chamber leaks. The control system will automatically shut down when dangerous conditions are approaching and ask the user to fix the issue before proceeding and display the warning screen as shown in Figure 2(d).  
      1. Maximum limit for hydrostatic pressure input: 3 atm (pressure limit requested by sponsor) and if the pressure is sensed to leak 0.1 atm/sec, system operations are paused and warning displayed)  
      2. Maximum limit for electric field input: 5V/cm (safety limit before unintended electrolysis occurs).  
      3. Maximum limit for magnetic field density input: 15 Gauss (to avoid overheating of the coils).  
         1. Thermistors detect overheating of the coils (if temperature exceeds 50 degrees Celsius, the system operations pause and warning is displayed)  
         2. Hall sensors verify that the input magnetic field for each chamber matches the actual output within a \+/-1 Gauss tolerance. If outside this tolerance, the user is warned to check system connections and housing for any interference with the magnetic coils.  
   3. When a user finishes an experiment, they can click “save” to automatically save images and data to a folder. (the “record” button shown in Figure 2(c)-(d) changes to “save” when data recordings and image capture is complete)

2. Touchscreen interface on the MCCB

![][image50]  
Figure 3\. Touchscreen interface on the MCCB with a USB port for uploading data and image recordings to a USB flash drive. (Note: image features the MCCB prototype from the previous MAE 156B team)

1. A touchscreen display would be integrated directly onto the MCCB. The touchscreen compatible with a Raspberry Pi microcontroller connected to the MCCB electronics would have an embedded processing system to provide both input and visualization, allowing the user to adjust stimulus parameters, control gantry movement, and monitor live camera images directly from the device.  
   2. The same safety constraints from the external computer option would be provided for the touchscreen control interface. Also, to avoid any chamber fluids splashing on the screen, the touchscreen should be placed above the well base.  
   3. The images and data are saved in folders and can be uploaded to a USB flash drive connected to the USB port shown in Figure 3\.

3. Game controller interface built into the MCCB  
   ![][image51]  
   Figure 4\. Game controller user interface built into the MCCB. Control descriptions labeled for the joystick and buttons.  
     
   1. This option uses mechanical controls such as a joystick and buttons from a game controller to control system functions as shown in Figure 4\. The game controller joystick could be used for manual control of gantry translation while buttons can switch chamber selections for applying stimuli, activate stimuli, and start image recording. A display screen would still be required to show the settings, sensor readings, and microscope images, but the display would no longer be touchscreen. The game controller must be compatible with an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi microcontroller that connects to the MCCB electronics on the top of the well base.  
   2. The same safety constraints built into the external computer and touchscreen interface options would be provided for the game controller interface.  
   3. The images and data can be uploaded to a USB flash drive.

Summary and Recommendations for MCCB Design Integration Considerations  
The three user interface options were evaluated using performance metrics derived from the MCCB functional requirements including data organization capability, safety implementation reliability, gantry motion control, integration risk near fluidic chambers, development complexity, and system cost. Based on the comparative analysis, the software program on an external computer is the most suitable user interface option for the MCCB when considering factors such as cost, complexity, and interface flexibility. This approach is low-cost and easiest to debug when issues arise as the program can be directly edited on the computer software. This approach also allows for larger and higher quality display screens assuming a quality computer is available to avoid purchasing a separate display screen for the touchscreen or game controller options. However, it is important to further discuss with the team if a self-contained system is preferred and safe to implement. For the case of a self-contained system, the game controller is the better choice considering that it is more flexible and lower cost than the touchscreen option for integration with the well base structure. If the well base design goes through changes in prototype iterations, the touchscreen housing would also have to change to be safely placed away from the fluidic chambers whereas the game controller just requires a wire connection and no separate housing. Additionally, the game controller is more flexible than the touchscreen for interface updates as the function of the joystick and buttons remains the same for any display changes whereas the touchscreen selections would need to be reprogrammed for display changes. Performance metrics and weightings are summarized below:

| Performance Metric | Weight | Rationale |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Safety sensor implementation and reliability \+ UI compatibility | High | Crossing safety boundaries discussed in functional requirements can damage cell cultures as well as the MCCB system itself |
| Ease of gantry control | medium | Required for capturing images, but translation precision is not a primary concern |
| Integration risk near fluids | medium | Electronics must be protected from potential fluid leaks and spills |
| Development complexity | medium | Project timeline favors simpler implementation and flexible UI to debug and update |
| Portability | Low | Self-contained operation is not an explicit requirement, but rather an extra feature |
| Ease of data organization | High | Images and sensor data with corresponding chamber and stimuli conditions must be easily stored and accessed |
| Cost | Medium | High quality sensors are prioritized in electronics budget, therefore UI cost should be on the lower end |

Among the evaluated options, the software interface on an external computer carries the most benefits across comparative metrics. However, a further discussion with the status of the MCCB design is required to determine if a self-contained game-controller system is worth the additional complexities, lead time, and cost involved.

#### **Gantry System  (by Dylan Lee)**

Project Description  
The overall goal of the Multi-chamber bioreactor is to subject a stem cell culture to specific electromagnetic stimuli and observe the response of the cells. Observation is done by 4 camera-microscope modules that look through the bottom of the cell culture wells. The gantry is what enables the modules to move around below the wells, allowing observation of specific cells and positioning for long periods of fixed observation.

A gantry in essence is a robotic system capable of moving a toolhead in 2 or 3 axes over a workspace. Its primary advantage over other workpiece manipulation tools is in not needing to accelerate/move the workpiece itself, which can cause issues if the piece is heavy or sensitive to movement. 3d printers, pick-and-place machines, and CNC mills all use this technology in order to achieve their dynamic flexibility. \[1\]

The microscope gantry is the structural and mechanical assembly below the bioreactor that holds one microscope and camera assembly per well, keeping it a fixed distance from the bottom of the wells to maintain a precise focal length to the relevant samples. We are currently waiting on the sponsor to decide his preferred viewing apparatus, only after which we can quantitatively define the focal length. The gantry allows fine control over where exactly the microscope is looking, allowing for small alignment adjustments and the capability to move the microscope to track a sample in real-time.

With the functional requirements listed below taken into consideration, the pool of mechanical options was narrowed to the following 3: A stepper motor belt-driven system (fig.1), a stepper motor driven leadscrew system (fig.2,3), and a system that utilizes prebuilt linear actuators (fig.4,5).

![][image57]  
Figure 1\. A 3-axis gantry system personally designed and built several years ago that used 3 independent belt drive systems to drive the axes.

![][image58]![][image59]

Figure 2 (left). The leadscrew z-axis mechanism on the ender 3 3d printer. The stepper motor drives the leadscrew directly and the leadscrew nut is mounted to the x-axis stage. \[12\]  
Figure 3 (right). A rough diagram of a gantry system utilizing leadscrews and stepper motors.  
![][image60]

Figure 4\. Actuonix P16-P Linear Actuator with Feedback 50mm travel. One of the suggested parts for achieving linear motion in the gantry. \[11\]  
![][image61]  
Figure 5\. Proposed mechanism that utilizes two linear actuators to construct a two-axis gantry

Functional Requirements

1. 2 degrees of freedom to traverse between a grid of wells  
2. Can be controlled through an electronic digital or joystick interface (so driven by motors, not manually)  
3. Sufficient precision in both axes to view individual embryo  
   1. 700μm is the typical embryo width, so \<100μm/count is the desired precision  
4. Capable of holding position for 7 days straight  
   1. generating enough resistive torque to withstand \~300N of force from table vibrations and accidental hand hits  
   2. Max divergence from original position is \<100μm (one motor step)  
   3. No perceptible sample disruption from motor position hold vibration  
5. No major sample disruption during traversal  
   1. Determined by measuring acoustics, \<55dB rated noise output at 45 cm  
6. Simplicity: can be fully developed with enough time for testing in one quarter

Component Options:

MOTOR CHOICE FOR COMPARISON: NEMA 17 Stepper motor \[2\]: 

* 0.9 degree/step  
  * 46 Ncm  
  * 3500 RPM at high torque  
* Leadscrew and nut with linear rails (including linear rod hardware) \[3\] \[4\] \[5\] \[6\] \[7\]: $497.06  
  * Nut threads to the microscope block, and inner threads interface with the leadscrew attached to the motor shaft. When the motor spins, the nut travels linearly along the leadscrew.  
  * ⅜” diameter rod  
  * 0.063” travel per rotation  
    * 3.97 μm/step  
  * 40% torque efficiency, standard for acme threads \[13\]  
    * \~675 N braking force  
  * Up to \~16” effective travel  
  * Backlash unknown (non-standard ACME thread type), however it would require over 22.7 degrees of rotational deadband to exceed maximum allowable positional error. This is both unreasonable and physically impossible.  
* 16T GT2 Belt drive system (including linear rod hardware) \[5\] \[6\] \[7\] \[8\] \[9\]: $405.51  
  * The stepper motor has a pulley on the drive shaft, which moves a belt. The microscope block is attached to this belt.  
  * 32mm pitch circumference  
    * Translates to 80μm travel/step  
  * \>95% torque efficiency for GT2 \[10\]  
    * \~90N braking force  
  * Travel limited by assembly, not belt  
* Actuonix P16-P Linear Actuator with Feedback 50mm travel (including linear rod hardware) \[5\] \[6\] \[7\] \[11\]: $546.12  
  * All-in-one module with a piston-like arm that extends and retracts linearly with closed-loop position control  
  * 50mm travel  
  * 500N backdriving floor  
  * 0.3mm repeatability/backlash: \~300μm effective precision  
  * Does not use the NEMA 17  
  * 62 dB noise output at 45 cm

Comparison Table

| Item | Pros | Cons |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Leadscrew and Nut ($497.06) | 1 day mcmaster shipping Highest precision at \~4μm/step Sufficiently resists accidental backdriving with \>500N resistance | Leadscrews come in inconvenient sizes (nothing between 18” and 12”) Noise output level unknown |
| 16t GT2 Belt pulley system ($405.51) | Cheapest method 1 day amazon prime shipping Lightest assembly \~1.8m/s top speed, more agile than other options Sufficient precision at 80μm/step | Requires designing complex belt tensioning setups. \[10\] Lower precision than leadscrew Insufficient torque to brake against accidental hits (90N\<500N) Noise output level unknown |
| Linear Actuator ($546.12) | Simplest all-in-one design Closed-loop control simplifies software needs Sufficiently resists accidental backdriving with 500N resistance | Does not meet precision targets, off by a factor of 3 Most expensive option Much harder to find at common retailers, shipping will be longer and more expensive Noise output level above 55 dB requirement (62 dB) |

	The Leadscrew and Nut mechanism yields the most promise among the 3 options. It fulfills each of the design requirements while taking advantage of the quality mcmaster customer service and it is simpler to design around than the belt pulley system. It is also the industry standard for mechanisms like this, as mechanisms like CNC routers and mills use leadscrews for precise movements. The only issue up in the air is whether the vibrations from the motors will cause disruption in the sample medium. This will need to be tested physically, and approved by the sponsor, who currently does not have a quantitative rating for how still the sample should be. There is an opportunity for significant noise reduction through Trinamic stealth stepper motor drivers, which have been proven to reduce stepper noise by up to 10 dB \[14\]. Despite the starting value being unknown, this does increase confidence that a solution can be found within the leadscrew mechanism if the vibrations become a problem.

#### **Well Design  (by Samantha Olivar)**

Project Description  
The Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor’s (MCCB) intended purpose is to apply external stimuli—specifically magnetic and electric fields—to cell cultures and observe the effects on the cells over time using a microscope and camera. A bioreactor is defined as a device used to cultivate living material in a controlled environment to produce altered biological products \[1\]. However, while typical bioreactors can start around $20000 \[2\], our MCCB design aims to provide a bioreactor tool to our sponsor that is more affordable and tailored to his needs.

![][image62]  
Figure 1\. MCCB cross-sectional diagram highlighting the well design interface with other system components, with a red-dashed line representing the unobstructed optical path for microscope observation

An important component of our bioreactor is the component holding the cells—the well design, as highlighted in Figure 1\. The cell well serves as the fundamental interface of the entire system, as it acts as the primary containment for a saline-cell solution and will interface with the lid to create isolated stimulus chambers. As seen by the dashed red line in Figure 1, a microscope-camera system will be situated underneath the wells to observe the effects on the cells over time. Therefore, the bottom of the well must have optical clarity and must not leak. Additionally, the well material must not interfere with the magnetic and electric stimuli applied to the cells. The design of the wells is a crucial part of the bioreactor, as it holds the primary target of observation and must be designed to interact with the other components of the MCCB, such as the microscope, the stimulus generators, and the lid design.

Functional Requirements

1. Wells must be able to be adapted for a multi-well layout  
   1. The system must contain a minimum of 4 wells to allow for simultaneous test environments.  
2. Individual well dimensions  
   1. Each well shall have a minimum internal diameter of 2 cm to accommodate different input nozzles and electrodes.  
   2. Each well shall have a minimum internal height of 1 cm to provide sufficient space for the cell cultures.  
3. The bottom surface of each well shall be optically transparent to be compatible with a x100 magnification microscope \[3\]  
   1. The well bottom shall be constructed of a material that has \>95% light transmission and \<2% haze.  
   2. The well bottom must have a thickness of 0.17 \+/- 0.01 mm (See Appendix B)  
4. Each well shall include a sealing surface that is compatible with the lid design to form independent micro-environments  
   1. To prevent evaporative loss, cross-contamination, and the loss of the cell culture, the leakage rate shall not exceed 5.6 g/hr \[4\]  
5. All materials used should be biocompatible  
   1. All materials in contact with the cell culture shall be certified non-toxic to cells, meeting ISO 10993-5 standards.

Component Options  
To meet the requirements for optical transparency (FR 3\) and sealing (FR 4), three distinct fabrication methods were evaluated, along with additional sealing method considerations. Supporting data and manufacturer specifications are included in Appendix B.

Fabrication Options:

1. Custom machining wells with a bonded optical slide at the bottom

This method requires CNC machining the wells from CAD models and then bonding a microscope optical-grade slide to the bottom using a biocompatible glue. It also allows us to specify the dimensions as necessary to meet our needs. With this method, we can choose from various sealing options and customize the lid design by designing the well and lid in parallel, rather than designing a lid to fit a pre-chosen well design with specific features. Figure 2 demonstrates a CAD model of a well with exterior threads. that can be paired with a lid. Using Fusion360, operations can be specified in order to make the well on a CNC machine.

![][image63]  
Figure 2\. CAD model of a custom well in Fusion360

2. Modifying commercially available cell wells

This approach involves us mechanically modifying off-the-shelf containers to fit within the intended MCCB and interface with all the other components. Depending on what we purchase, the amount of modification needed may vary. While using a standard biological grade cell culture dish will satisfy FR 3 immediately, modification will be needed to meet FR 4\. As seen in Figure 3(a), the lid cannot securely interface with the well because it is meant to be removed and viewed from overhead. However, if a jar with a prepared sealing interface, as seen in Figure 3(b) were used, modifications would need to be made to satisfy FR 3 because the bottom would not be optically clear. Additionally, even though the jar would have a threaded interface, additional work may be required to fully satisfy FR 4 because the lid would need to be precisely designed to match the threads, or a purchasable lid would need to have holes added to allow for fluid inputs and electrodes.

(a)![][image64](b)![][image65]  
Figure 3\. (a) FisherSci Cell Culture Dish (b) Containers\&Packaging 1/4 oz natural-colored PP plastic single-wall jar

3. 3D resin printing wells to have an embedded glass window

Resin printing the wells would require printing with a biocompatible resin and post-print attaching an optically clear slide to the bottom. This method would allow for rapid prototyping and manufacturing, given that a CAD is prepared beforehand. The critical constraint for this method would be to satisfy FR 5.1 because most resin printing materials are not biocompatible. Therefore, a sterilization process or the use of biocompatible resin in a 3D machine reserved for biocompatible resin would be required.

Sealing Options (see diagrams in Appendix B)  
To satisfy FR 4.1, different sealing methods were also evaluated.

1. O-ring: O-rings are rubber rings used to prevent leakage, and existing standards outline the dimensioning of these rings and the grooves needed for them.  
   1. Axial (Face) O-ring Seal: Compression in the axial direction will press against the O-ring to seal the well against the lid. A groove would be needed in the lid or the face of the well. This method is best incorporated with a compression sealing method rather than a threaded twisting seal, because the twisting forces could distort the placement of the O-ring.  
   2. Radial (Bore) O-ring Seal: The O-ring would be installed on the outer diameter of the portion of the lid that slots into the well, requiring a groove in the lid, but not the well. This option would be more suitable for a threaded screw interface between the lid because it is less sensitive to torque than an axial O-ring seal.  
2. Gasket: A gasket is a thin sheet of a rubber-like material compressed between a lid and a face on the container. Gaskets do not require specialized groove machining like O-rings.

Summary

| Well Options | Pros | Cons | Estimated Cost (including shipping) | Shipping Time |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Custom machining of polycarbonate wells | Fully customizable geometry Mechanical stability Allows for a definable interface with the lid | Adhesive Failure Risks Long manufacturing time (machining 1 prototype took \>5 hours, including CNC coding and physically machining) | Polycarbonate \~ $40 Glass slides \~$20 Adhesive \~$100 | 2-3 weeks (for all materials |
| Modifying commercially available cell wells (Cell Culture Dishes) (Jars) | Professional optical quality Limited fabrication needed to establish optical clarity Pre-established Sealing interface Limited fabrication needed to establish a sealing interface Cost-effective | Limited customization allowed Requires more fabrication for the lid to satisfy FR 4 Standard well geometries lack dedicated compression surfaces for airtight seals Requires fabrication to satisfy FR 3 Injection-molded jars have high inaccuracies with manufacturing that will lead to difficulties when designing the lid | \~$300 (only able to buy in bulk \- with no further inquiry, may be able to get smaller quantities) jars  $40 Adhesive \~$100 | 5-8 days |
| 3D resin printing wells | Rapid prototyping High design flexibility | Extensive post-processing is needed on the in-house resin to satisfy FR 5.1 Specific, less cost-effective resin needed to satisfy FR 5.1 | Resin print \~$50 (using in-house materials) Resin print \~$500 (buying specialized resin) Glass slides \~$20 Adhesive \~$100 | \<1 day (in-house) 1 week (ordering specific resin) |

Evaluating the three options against the functional requirements for the well design, the cost, and the interface with other components of the MCCB, the CNC-machined wells are the most technically viable solution. This approach provides the mechanical rigidity and design necessary to maintain a seal and give our team the dimensional precision required to interface the well with the lid and other components. CNC machining the wells also allows for the integration of standard O-ring glands. While the specific sealing method (O-rings and gaskets) will need to be determined later after further consideration, the customizability of this option allows us to adapt to a specific sealing method. While the 3D printed option is appealing because of the rapid prototyping, there are significant risks considering the material and satisfying FR 5.1. Modifying commercial wells would be the lowest-ranked option because of the difficulties in manufacturing a seal for the optically clear wells on the market, and because of the variations in the sealing interface that would make it difficult later on, as we need to design a matching lid.  
Because the well design will determine the lid design, it is an influential part of the system. It must interact with the other components to ensure there is an appropriate seal on the chamber while allowing for the various stimuli and observation indicated in Figure 1\.

AI/LLM Usage  
Optical Clarity Inquiry

AI Input:

How can I quantify the engineering requirement that a cell well bottom must allow it's contents to be observable by a 100x magnification microscope?

AI Output:

To quantify the engineering requirement for microscopic observability at $100\\times$ magnification, you must define the optical and mechanical interface between the well bottom and the microscope objective. High-magnification objectives, particularly $100\\times$ oil-immersion lenses, have extremely shallow depths of field and short working distances, making generic "transparency" insufficient for a functional requirement. \[1, 2\]

## ***1\. Optical Thickness and Tolerance*** {#1.-optical-thickness-and-tolerance}

Standard high-magnification objectives are optically corrected for a specific thickness of material, typically a \#1.5 coverslip. \[3, 4\]

* Target Value: $0.17 \\text{ mm}$ (170 $\\mu\\text{m}$).  
* Tolerance: $\\pm 0.005 \\text{ mm}$ (5 $\\mu\\text{m}$) for high-precision applications.  
* Why: Deviating from this thickness causes spherical aberration, which degrades image resolution and contrast, especially at high Numerical Apertures (NA). \[5, 6\]

## ***2\. Refractive Index ($n\_D$)*** {#2.-refractive-index-($n_d$)}

The material must match the refractive index for which the objective was designed to prevent light from bending (refracting) at the interface. \[7\]

* Target Value: $1.52 \\pm 0.01$.  
* Materials: Borosilicate glass or specialized cyclic olefin polymers (COP) are often used to meet this index while remaining non-toxic. \[8\]

## ***3\. Working Distance ($WD$)*** {#3.-working-distance-($wd$)}

The "Working Distance" is the physical gap between the front of the lens and the top of the well bottom.

* Quantification: The total thickness of your well bottom must be significantly less than the $WD$ of a standard $100\\times$ objective, which is often as low as $0.13 \\text{ mm}$ to $0.23 \\text{ mm}$.  
* Constraint: If your well bottom is $0.5 \\text{ mm}$ thick, a $100\\times$ objective literally cannot get close enough to focus on the cells. \[9, 10, 11\]

## ***4\. Surface Roughness ($R\_a$) and Flatness*** {#4.-surface-roughness-($r_a$)-and-flatness}

Scattered light from a rough surface will ruin high-resolution imaging. \[12\]

* Surface Roughness: $R\_a \< 10 \\text{ nm}$ (typically "optical grade" finish).  
* Flatness: Global flatness across the multi-well plate should be within $\\pm 50 \\mu\\text{m}$ to avoid the need for constant refocusing when moving between wells. \[13\]

## ***Summary Table for revision:*** {#summary-table-for-revision:}

| Parameter | Quantitative Value | Reference Standard |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Material Thickness | $0.17 \\text{ mm} \\pm 0.01 \\text{ mm}$ | [\#1.5 Coverslip Standard](https://evidentscientific.com/en/microscope-resource/knowledge-hub/anatomy/specifications) |
| Refractive Index ($n\_D$) | $1.52 \\pm 0.02$ | [Borosilicate/D-263 Glass](https://ibidi.com/content/387-microscopy-parameters-of-surfaces) |
| Surface Finish ($R\_a$) | $\\leq 15 \\text{ nm}$ | Optical Polish |
| Autofluorescence | $\\leq 5\\%$ of signal | Low-fluorescence Grade |

---

Answer

To quantify the "observability" requirement, you should specify the well bottom as having a thickness of $0.17 \\pm 0.01 \\text{ mm}$ and a refractive index of $1.52$, matching the industry standard for \#1.5 coverslips. This ensures the objective lens can physically reach the focal plane and maintain the resolution required for $100\\times$ magnification.

Would you like to see a drafted test procedure for verifying these optical tolerances in a lab setting?

Important Insights:

* O-rings are often the “go-to” sealing technology in the Navy for their operations and in his experience, because of their robustness and their ability to withstand up to 15000 psi in most cases  
* Design configurations for O-rings must be considered when designing the interface for the lid  
  * Face seals are typically used for compression sealing. Using a face seal with a twist-in cap, as we did in our initial designs for risk reduction, can lead to distortion or misalignment of the O-ring, often disrupting the seal  
  * Bore seals are more ideal for sliding motion (twisting, especially for a screw-in lid) between parts  
* Gaskets are a viable alternative for flat face operations and can be considered in our design, especially if we are only using them for low-pressure applications  
* O-rings are often standard and there is a handbook (Parker O-ring handbook) that can be used to size O-rings appropriately. The most challenging part of implementing an O-ring seal would be the precision required to machine the groove and achieve the correct compression

## ***A.6 User Manual*** {#a.6-user-manual}

### **Description of Device** {#description-of-device}

	The Multi-Chamber Bioreactor is a biology research platform used to simultaneously stimulate and image cell cultures over long periods of time. Everything is controlled through the central raspberry pi 5, and the apparatus is capable of electric field stimulation, magnetic field stimulation, or both at once.

### **List of Components** {#list-of-components}

###### **Table A.6.1 \- List of Components included in the System** {#table-a.6.1---list-of-components-included-in-the-system}

| Item \# | Item | Amount | Image |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----- |
| 1 | Assembled Chassis | 1 | ![][image75] |
| 2 | Well Body | 4 | ![][image76] |
| 3 | Well Lid | 4 | ![][image77] |
| 4 | Helmholtz Coil | 4 | ![][image78] |
| 5 | Microscope Mount | 4 | ![][image79] |
| 6 | Optics Train \+ Camera | 1\* | ![][image80] |
| 7 | Raspberry Pi Touchscreen | 1 | **![][image81]** |
| 8 | 24 V Power Supply | 1 | ![][image82] |

\* final system will have 4 after the sponsor buys additional microscopes and cameras but for this project, they were not provided or in budget

### **Warnings and Safety Precautions** {#warnings-and-safety-precautions}

To avoid injury or damage to the equipment, please read the following:

1. Electrical devices  
   1. 24V DC is present on many semi-exposed wires. While safe to touch, ensure that NO SALINE is present on electronic components and make contact with any of these wires to prevent shorts from occurring.  
2. Heat on components  
   1. Extended length testing shows the electromagnet reaches up to 60 degrees Celsius under maximum operating conditions. Refrain from touching the electromagnet components during operation, and allow them to cool down for at least 10 minutes before touching them to manipulate the apparatus.  
   2. At max power output, the DRV8876 motor drivers on the protoboard can reach temperatures of upwards of 120 degrees Celsius on the main IC, and theoretically, thermal throttling only takes effect at a maximum of 180 degrees Celsius. Do not touch the board or IC during operation.  
   3. To allow for effective convection cooling, do not attempt to cover the electronics or electrodes.  
3. Toxic components and corrosion  
   1. Exposed copper from electronics and electromagnet wire can corrode easily in the presence of saline solution. Avoid splashing on any components at any time, and if splashing does happen, dry off the parts immediately.  
   2. Although unlikely, if the electromagnet shorts to the 24V power supply, the coil will quickly exceed 120 degrees Celsius and begin deforming and melting the ASA housing. ASA plastic releases toxic fumes when heated to temperatures as low as 140 degrees Celsius. Be aware of any strange smells coming from the MCCB.  
   3. All board electronics use leaded solder to assemble the board. Do not touch the electronics directly to avoid potential lead contamination and poisoning.  
4. Electrolysis risk  
   1. Electrodes in a saline solution have a chance of performing electrolysis. Although the peak theoretical voltage achievable is too low to perform electrolysis, if bubbles appear to form on the electrode inside the solution, turn off the system to avoid sample toxification.  
5. Sharp edges  
   1. Ends of the aluminum t-slot extrusions and other parts of the MCCB may have sharp corners. Avoid dragging hands over surfaces and be aware of parts jutting out.  
6. Acrylic weight capacity  
   1. Do not place additional items on top of the acrylic sheet. It is not designed to bear additional load, and it will influence the focus of the microscopes.  
7. Eddy currents  
   1. A switching magnetic field generates eddy currents in nearby metal objects, which heats it up and disrupts the field. Do not place metal objects near an enabled electromagnet.  
8. Glass Wells  
   1. The bottom of the wells is a thin glass slide. Do not slam the well onto a hard or uneven surface, as this may shatter the glass. If shattered, dispose of the well in the appropriate receptacle.  
9. Well Lid Plunger  
   1. The central plunger attached to the lid is hollow at the intersection of the plunger and the lid to accommodate the LED. Do not apply excessive force at the tip of the plunger as this may cause it to snap.

### **Operation Steps** {#operation-steps}

#### **For Initial Loading of Samples**

1. Power off the MCCB completely  
2. Disconnect electrode and LED cable from PCB  
3. Remove well from the electromagnet cavity, pulling out wire  
4. Unscrew the lid  
5. Sterilize the well by any means the user deems necessary  
6. Add new saline and cell sample to well (can also be added   
7. Holding the lid, twist the well back onto the assembly  
8. Insert the well into the electromagnet cavity  
9. Connect the LED and electrode wires to the PCB  
10. Repeat steps 2-9 for every well that will be used for the current run  
11. Power on the MCCB  
12. Manually adjust the microscopes to view the sample clearly  
13. Set power and frequency for each electrode and electromagnet  
14. Start recording

### **General Tips** {#general-tips}

* The USB3.0 bus that transfers the microscope camera streams is not enough for 4 60fps 1.6MP feeds. If running into issues streaming 4 cameras at once, lower the framerate and resolution.  
* The well only fits into the electromagnet two out of the four possible ways. If it does not fit, rotate it 90 degrees and try again.  
* Do not unplug the electromagnet from the board. The connector is identical to the electrode connector, and if they are switched, putting 24V through the electrode will kill the sample and damage the component.  
* The emergency stop simply kills power to the entire MCCB. This will lead to video data corruption, so use only after the Pi has been shut down or in emergencies.

# **Executive Summary**

# **Executive Summary \- Multi-chamber Camera Bioreactor**

Sponsor: Peter Chen  
Dylan Bailes, Kaitlyn Lavarias, Dylan Lee, Samantha Olivar  
MAE 156B \- Fundamental Principles of Mechanical Design II  
University of California San Diego  
Professor David Gillett

## ***Project Background and Motivation***

This project, sponsored by researcher Peter Chen, provides a research platform for analyzing stem cell differentiation behavior in the presence of external stimuli. Based on specific stimuli, a stem cell can be encouraged to switch to different development modes in a process called differentiation, allowing them to be used for applications like limb regrowth or other regenerative medical procedures. Exposure to electric and magnetic fields are stimuli that have proven effects, however the data on what exactly those effects are is ambiguous. The goal of the equipment is to house multiple stem cell cultures inside wells filled with saline fluid and subject them to controlled electric fields via titanium electrodes and magnetic fields through Helmholtz electromagnet coils. 

## ***Project Objectives***

The team developed a system that:

1. Houses cell cultures within a leak-proof sterile environment with real-time system monitoring via a user-friendly interface  
2. Stimulates the 0.9% saline solution cell culture with a variable electric field ranging from 0-1.5 V/cm and a variable magnetic field ranging from 0-5 mT  
3. Has integrated imaging of the individual cells through an optical train attached to a camera

## ***Final Design Solution***

## ***![][image83]***

##### **Figure 1 \- Functional Block Diagram of the Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor System**

Figure 1 outlines the interaction between all the system components included in the Multi-Chamber Camera Bioreactor design. The physical system of the MCCB, shown in Figure 2, will hold the cell cultures in a configuration that allows them to be subjected to electric and magnetic fields. Inlets and outlets in the wells will allow for fluidic cell cultures to be manually inserted into the chambers using a syringe. For comparison, a photo of the fabricated system is shown in Figure 3, including all the electronics and the touchscreen interface that controls the system. Individual camera-microscope modules on fine-control 3-axis gantry systems have been positioned below each well, allowing clear vision at specific points of interest inside each cell culture.

![][image84]

##### **Figure 2 Full CAD Assembly of the MCCB**

##### ![][image85]

**Figure 3 Full Photo Assembly of the MCCB**  
	  
	Figure 4 shows a labeled assembly of the well components, highlighting the titanium plate electrodes slotted into the wall of the chamber and the o-ring in the dovetail groove on the top face. The square impression on the bottom of the well leaves room for a cover glass slide that will provide optical clarity to allow for clear microscope imaging.

 ![][image86]

##### **Figure 4 Full CAD assembly of the well body**

Wells were designed around manufacturing using the Stratasys polyjet 3D printer, allowing for custom features like slots for the electrodes, a threaded and sealable lid, as well as mating features for luer locks that allow the user to manually add additional saline fluid during the experiment. 

![][image87]  
**Figure 5 User Interface Control Home Screen where users can see an overview of the different stimuli per well.**

 The User Interface home screen is shown in Figure 5 and will be displayed on a touch screen which allows the user to dictate the magnitude of electric and magnetic fields applied to the cell cultures, also allowing for the individual control of each of the 4 wells within the MCCB. In order to monitor the electric field and magnetic field current sensors and hall sensors provides feedback to the UI, to inform and calibrate the user input settings. The camera attachments on the microscopes image the effects on the target cells over time, allowing for automated imaging via the user interface touchscreen.

## ***Project Success and Impact***

By providing a cost-effective, customizable, and user-friendly platform, this project successfully lowers the barrier to entry for advanced electrobiology research. The system’s physical performance was verified through direct voltage mapping, magnetometer measurements, current monitoring, and Maxwell simulations. The testing and verification confirmed the generation and accuracy of the required uniform electric fields between 0-1.5 V/cm and magnetic fields between 0-5 mT. Furthermore, pressure testing validated that the modeled threads profiles and o-ring maintained a leak-proof environment. Ultimately, the successful integration of real time microscopy and validated stimuli controls delivers a functional user-friendly tool for cell differentiation research. With the MCCB, bioengineers can make new discoveries in regenerative medicine by observing how cells respond to the fundamental forces of electricity and magnetism.

**Table 1.- This is a good table, it gives clear comparison points and explains how the different designs work, it could be better if the "how it works" column wouldn't be that wordy**

| Design | Main Components | How it works |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Counter  Rotating  | A nested shaft A secondary rotary motor Lead screw assembly | The inner pipe of the nested shaft system would be connected to a secondary rotary motor that would rotate to counteract the rotation caused by the current motor system. This secondary motor (and a pair of bearings) would be connected to the linear motor such that the two systems would move in tandem with one another. The lead screw system would position the transducer radially. |
| Double  Nested Shaft | Secondary and tertiary rotary motor A double nested shaft (three shafts within one another) Bevel gears A lead screw | The most inner shaft would be actuated by the smallest rotary motor available which would rotate bevel gears that connect to a lead screw to translate the transducer radially. The next inner shaft would be actuated by the next motor to rotate the entire transducer platform for rotational placement of the transducer. With the use of bearings the shafts would be rigidly connected such that only one connection to the linear motor would move all the shafts. |
| Single Nested Spline  | A secondary rotary motor A nested shaft Lead screw Spline shaft | With the use of a spline, the secondary motor is rigidly connected to the table at an appropriate height. The spline was the inner shaft to the nested shaft system. Actuated by that motor the spline would rotate to rotationally place the transducer. With the use of bearings, the shafts will translate in tandem. The lead screw would be actuated by a DC motor that would translate the transducer radially. |
